metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: It's the butterfly effect. It's basically that in the short term, you can predict something extremely

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: well by knowing the current state of the system. But a few steps down, it's very hard to predict

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: based on the current knowledge. Is that because the system is truly free? When I look at weather

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: patterns, I can predict the next 10 days. Is it because the weather has a lot of freedom?

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: And after 10 days, it chooses to do something else? Or is it because in fact, the system is

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: fully deterministic and there's just a slightly different magnetic field of the earth, slightly

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: more energy arriving from the sun, a slightly different spin of the gravitational pull of Jupiter

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: that is now causing all kinds of tides and slight deviation of the moon, et cetera. Maybe all of that

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: can be fully modeled. Maybe the fact that China is emitting a little more carbon today is actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: going to affect the weather in Egypt in three weeks. And all of that could be fully modeled.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: In the same way, if you take a complete view of a human being now, I model everything about you,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: the question is, can I predict your next step? Probably. But at how far? And if it's a little

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: further, is that because of stochasticity and chaos properties of unpredictability of beyond

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: a certain level, or was that actually true free will? Yeah. So the number of variables might be

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: so... You might need to build an entire universe to be able to model. To simulate a human. And then

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: maybe that human will be fully simulatable, but maybe aspects of free will will exist. And where's

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: that free will coming from? It's still coming from the same neurons or maybe from a spirit

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: inhabiting these neurons. But again, it's very difficult empirically to evaluate where does

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: free will begin and sort of chemical reactions and electric signals end. So on that topic,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: let me ask the most absurd question that most MIT faculty rolled their eyes on. But

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: what do you think about the simulation hypothesis and the idea that we live in a simulation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: I think it's complete BS. There's no empirical evidence. No, it's not. Absolutely none.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: Not in terms of empirical evidence, but in terms of a thought experiment, does it help you think

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: about the universe? I mean, so if you look at the genome, it's encoding a lot of the information

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: that is required to create some of the beautiful human complexity that we see around us. It's an

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: interesting thought experiment. How much parameters do we need to have in order to model this full

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: human experience? If we were to build a video game, how hard would it be to build a video game

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: that's convincing enough and fun enough and has consistent laws of physics, all that stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: It's not interesting to use a thought experiment. I mean, it's cute, but it's an occam's razor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: I mean, what's more realistic, the fact that you're actually a machine or that you're a person?

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: What's the fact that all of my experiences exist inside the chemical molecules that I have

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: or that somebody's actually simulating all that? Well, you did refer to humans as a digital computer

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: earlier. Of course, of course, but that does not- It's a kind of a machine, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: I know, I know, but I think the probability of all that is nil and let the machines wake me up and

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: just terminate me now if it's not. I challenge you machines. They're going to wait a little bit

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: to see what you're going to do next. It's fun. It's fun to watch, especially the clever humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: What's the difference to you between the way a computer stores information and the human genome

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: stores information? You also have roots and your work. Would you say when you introduce yourself

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: at a bar- It depends who I'm talking to. Would you say it's computational biology? Do you reveal

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: your expertise in computers? It depends who I'm talking to, truly. I mean, basically,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: if I meet someone who's in computers, I'll say, oh, I'm a professor in computer science.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: If I meet someone who's in engineering, I say computer science and electrical engineering.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: If I meet someone in biology, I'll say, hey, I work in genomics. If I meet someone in medicine,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: I'm like, hey, I work on genetics. You're a fun person meeting at a bar. I got you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: No, no. What I'm trying to say is that there's no single attribute that I will define myself as.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: There's a few things I know. There's a few things I study. There's a few things I have degrees on,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: and there's a few things that I grant degrees in. I publish papers across the whole gamut,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: the whole spectrum of computation to biology, et cetera. The complete answer is that I use

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: computer science to understand biology. I develop methods in AI and machine learning, statistics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: and algorithms, et cetera. But the ultimate goal of my career is to really understand biology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: If these things don't advance our understanding of biology, I'm not as fascinated by them. Although

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: there are some beautiful computational problems by themselves, I've made it my mission to apply

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: the power of computer science to truly understand the human genome, health, disease,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: and the whole gamut of how our brain works, how our body works, and all of that, which is so

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: fascinating. There's not an equivalent sort of complementary dream of understanding human biology

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: in order to create an artificial life, an artificial brain, an artificial intelligence

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: that supersedes the intelligence and the capabilities of us humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: It's an interesting question. It's a fascinating question. So understanding the human brain is

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: undoubtedly coupled to how do we make better AI, because so much of AI has in fact been inspired

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: by the brain. It may have taken 50 years since the early days of neural networks until we have

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: all of these amazing progress that we've seen with deep belief networks and all of these

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: advances in Go and Chess, in image synthesis, in deep fakes, in you name it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: But the underlying architecture is very much inspired by the human brain, which actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: posits a very, very interesting question. Why are neural networks performing so well?

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: And they perform amazingly well. Is it because they can simulate any possible function?

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: And the answer is no. No, they simulate a very small number of functions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: Is it because they can simulate every possible function in the universe?

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: And that's where it gets interesting. The answer is actually, yeah, a little closer to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: And here's where it gets really fun. If you look at human brain and human cognition,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: it didn't evolve in a vacuum. It evolved in a world with physical constraints,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: like the world that inhabits us. It is the world that we inhabit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: And if you look at our senses, what do they perceive? They perceive different parts of

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: the electromagnetic spectrum. The hearing is just different movements in air, the touch,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: etc. I mean, all of these things, we've built intuitions for the physical world that we inhabit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: And our brains and the brains of all animals evolved for that world. And so,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: the AI systems that we have built happen to work well with images of the type that we encounter in

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: the physical world that we inhabit. Whereas if you just take noise and you add random signal that

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: doesn't match anything in our world, neural networks will not do as well. And that actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: basically has this whole loop around this, which is this was designed by studying our

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: own brain, which was evolved for our own world, and they happen to do well in our own world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: And they happen to make the same types of mistakes that humans make many, many times.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: And of course, you can engineer images by adding just the right amount of pixel deviations to make

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: a zebra look like a bamboo and stuff like that, or like a table. But ultimately, the undocked images,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: at least, are very often mistaken, I don't know, between muffins and dogs, for example,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: in the same way that humans make those mistakes. So, there's no doubt in my view that the more we

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: understand about the tricks that our human brain has evolved to understand the physical world around

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: us, the more we will be able to bring new computational primitives in our AI systems

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: to, again, better understand not just the world around us, but maybe even the world inside us,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: and maybe even the computational problems that arise from new types of data that we haven't been

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: exposed to, but are yet inhabiting the same universe that we live in, with a very tiny little

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: subset of functions from all possible mathematical functions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: Yeah, and that small subset of functions, all that matters to us humans, really. That's what makes...

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: It's all that has mattered so far, but it's not the same thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: That's what makes... It's all that has mattered so far,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: and even within our scientific realm, it's all that seems to continue to matter. But, I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: I always like to think about our senses and how much of the physical world around us we perceive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: And if you look at the LIGO experiment over the last year and a half, it has been all over the news.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: What did LIGO do? It created a new sense for human beings, a sense that has never been sensed

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: in the history of our planet. Gravitational waves have been traversing the Earth

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: since its creation a few billion years ago. Life has evolved senses to sense things

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: that were never before sensed. Light was not perceived by early life. No one cared. And

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: eventually, photoreceptors evolved, and the ability to sense colors by sort of catching

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: different parts of that electromagnetic spectrum, and hearing evolved, and touch evolved, etc.

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: But no organism evolved a way to sense neutrinos floating through Earth or gravitational waves

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: flowing through Earth, etc. And I find it so beautiful in the history of not just humanity,

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: as the fact that we were blind to it is traumatizing before. Because that also tells us

metadata.title: Podcast: Manolis Kellis: Human Genome and Evolutionary Dynamics | Lex Fridman Podcast #113

body.input: It's beautiful, et cetera. But then there are intangible aspects of human communication

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: that our bots might meet?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: My hunch is no.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Most people say yes, absolutely.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I mean, and they'll cite the Drake equation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And I think in Singularity is Near,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I have two analyses of the Drake equation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: both with very reasonable assumptions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And one gives you thousands of advanced civilizations in each galaxy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And another one gives you one civilization,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: and we know of one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: A lot of the analyses are forgetting the exponential growth of computation

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: because we've gone from where the fastest way

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I could send a message to somebody was with a pony,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: which was what, like a century and a half ago?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: To the advanced civilization we have today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And if you accept what I've said, go forward a few decades,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: you're going to have an absolutely fantastic amount of civilization

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: compared to a pony, and that's in a couple hundred years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Yeah, the speed and the scale of information transfer

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: is just growing exponentially in a blink of an eye.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Now think about these other civilizations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: They're going to be spread out at cosmic times.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: So if something is like ahead of us or behind us,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: it could be ahead of us or behind us by maybe millions of years,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: which isn't that much.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I mean, the world is billions of years old, 14 billion or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: So even a thousand years, if two or 300 years is enough to go from a pony

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: to a fantastic amount of civilization, we would see that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: So of other civilizations that have occurred,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: some might be behind us, but some might be ahead of us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: If they're ahead of us, they're ahead of us by thousands, millions of years,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: and they would be so far beyond us,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: they would be doing galaxy-wide engineering.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: But we don't see anything doing galaxy-wide engineering.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: So either they don't exist or this very universe is a construction of an alien species.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: We're living inside a video game.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Well, that's another explanation that, yes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: you've got some teenage kids in another civilization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Do you find compelling the simulation hypothesis as a thought experiment

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: that we're living in a simulation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: The universe is computational, so we are an example in a computational world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Therefore, it is a simulation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: It doesn't necessarily mean an experiment by some high school kid in another world,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: but it nonetheless is taking place in a computational world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And everything that's going on is basically a form of computation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: So you really have to define what you mean by this whole world being a simulation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Well, then it's the teenager that makes the video game.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Us humans with our current limited cognitive capability

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: have strived to understand ourselves, and we have created religions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: We think of God.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Whatever that is, do you think God exists?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And if so, who is God?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I alluded to this before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: We started out with lots of particles going around.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And there's nothing that represents love and creativity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And somehow we've gotten into a world where love actually exists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And that has to do actually with consciousness,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: because you can't have love without consciousness.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: So to me, that's God, the fact that we have something where love,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: where you can be devoted to someone else and really feel that love, that's God.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And if you look at the Old Testament,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: it was actually created by several different rabbinets in there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And I think they've identified three of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: One of them dealt with God as a person that you can make deals with,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: and he gets angry, and he wrecks vengeance on various people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: But two of them actually talk about God as a symbol of love and peace and harmony and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: That's how they describe God.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: So that's my view of God, not as a person in the sky that you can make deals with.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: It's whatever the magic that goes from basic elements to things that consciousness and love.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Do you think one of the things I find extremely beautiful and powerful is cellular automata,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: which you also touch on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Do you think whatever the heck happens in cellular automata

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: where interesting, complicated objects emerge, God is in there too?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: The emergence of love in this seemingly primitive universe?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Well, that's the goal of creating a replicant,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: is that they would love you and you would love them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: There wouldn't be much point of doing it if that didn't happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: But all of it, I guess what I'm saying about cellular automata is it's primitive building blocks,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: and they somehow create beautiful things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Is there some deep truth to that about how our universe works?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: The emergence from simple rules, beautiful complex objects can emerge.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Is that the thing that made us as we went through all the six phases of reality?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: That's a good way to look at it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: It does make some point to the whole value of having a universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Do you think about your own mortality? Are you afraid of it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Yes, but I keep going back to my idea of being able to expand human life quickly enough

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: in advance of our getting there, longevity escape velocity,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: which we're not quite at yet, but I think we're actually pretty close,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: particularly with, for example, doing simulated biology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I think we can probably get there within, say, by the end of this decade, and that's my goal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Do you hope to achieve the longevity escape velocity? Do you hope to achieve immortality?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Well, immortality is hard to say. I can't really come on your program saying,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I've done it. I've achieved immortality because it's never forever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: A long time, a long time of living well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: But we'd like to actually advance human life expectancy, advance my life expectancy

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: more than a year every year.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And I think we can get there within by the end of this decade.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: How do you think we'd do it? So there's practical things in Transcend,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: the Nine Steps to Living Well Forever, your book, you describe just that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: There's practical things like health, exercise, all those things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Yeah, I mean, we live in a body that doesn't last forever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: There's no reason why it can't, though.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And we're discovering things, I think, that will extend it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: But you do have to deal with, I mean, I've got various issues.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Went to Mexico 40 years ago, developed Salmonella, I created pancreatitis,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: which gave me a strange form of diabetes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: It's not type 1 diabetes because that's an autoimmune disorder that destroys your pancreas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I don't have that. But it's also not type 2 diabetes because type 2 diabetes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: your pancreas works fine, but your cells don't absorb the insulin well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I don't have that either.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: The pancreatitis I had partially damaged my pancreas, but it was a one-time thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: It didn't continue. And I've learned now how to control it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: But so that's just something I had to do in order to continue to exist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Since your particular biological system, you had to figure out a few hacks

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: and the idea is that science would be able to do that much better, actually.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Yeah. So I mean, I do spend a lot of time just tinkering with my own body to keep it going.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: So I do think I'll last till the end of this decade, and I think we'll achieve longevity escape velocity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I think that will start with people who are very diligent about this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Eventually it'll become sort of routine that people will be able to do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: So if you're talking about kids today or even people in their 20s or 30s,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: it's really not a very serious problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I have had some discussions with relatives who were like almost 100 and saying,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: well, we're working on it as quickly as possible, but I don't know if that's going to work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Is there a case, this is a difficult question, but is there a case to be made against living forever,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: that a finite life, that mortality is a feature, not a bug, that living a shorter...

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: So dying makes ice cream taste delicious, makes life intensely beautiful more than it otherwise might be.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: People believe that way, except if you present a death of anybody they care about or love,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: they find that extremely depressing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And I know people who feel that way 20, 30, 40 years later, they still want them back.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I mean, death is not something to celebrate, but we've lived in a world where people just accept this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Life is short. You see it all the time on TV. Life's short. You have to take advantage of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And nobody accepts the fact that you can actually go beyond normal lifetimes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: But anytime we talk about death or a death of a person, even one death is a terrible tragedy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: If you have somebody that lives to 100 years old, we still love them in return.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And there's no limitation to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: In fact, these kinds of trends are going to provide greater and greater opportunity for everybody, even if we have more people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: So let me ask about an alien species or a super intelligent AI 500 years from now that will look back and remember Ray Kurzweil version zero,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: before the replicants spread. How do you hope they remember you in a Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy summary of Ray Kurzweil?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: What do you hope your legacy is?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Well, I mean, I do hope to be around. So that's some version of you. Yes. So you think you'll be the same person around?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I mean, am I the same person I was when I was 20 or 10?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: You would be the same person in that same way. But yes, we're different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: All we have of that, all you have of that person is your memories, which are probably distorted in some way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Maybe you just remember the good parts, depending on your psyche. You might focus on the bad parts, might focus on the good parts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Right. But I mean, I still have a relationship to the way I was when I was earlier, when I was younger.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: How will you and the other super intelligent AIs remember you of today from 500 years ago?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: What do you hope to be remembered by this version of you before the singularity?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Well, I think it's expressed well in my books, trying to create some new realities that people will accept.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I mean, that's something that gives me great pleasure and greater insight into what makes humans valuable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I'm not the only person who's tempted to comment on that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And optimism that permeates your work, optimism about the future.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Ultimately, that optimism paves the way for building a better future.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Yeah, I agree with that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: So you asked your dad about the meaning of life, and he said, love, let me ask you the same question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: What's the meaning of life? Why are we here?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: This beautiful journey they were on in phase four, reaching for phase five of this evolution and information processing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Why?

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I think I'd give the same answers as my father.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Because if there were no love and we didn't care about anybody, there'd be no point existing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Love is the meaning of life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: The AI version of your dad had a good point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Well, I think that's a beautiful way to end it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Thank you for your work. Thank you for being who you are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Thank you for dreaming about a beautiful future and creating it along the way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And thank you so much for spending a really valuable time with me today. This was awesome.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: Well, it's my pleasure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: And you have some great insights, both into me and into humanity as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ray Kurzweil: Singularity, Superintelligence, and Immortality | Lex Fridman Podcast #321

body.input: I appreciate that.
