body.input: up in the gizzard and polished and then left in a... So I like things that have been through

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: dramatic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: There's a story there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: There's a story.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: Yeah. I mean, that's okay. The really fascinating thing why seeing Allah or crosses in the stone,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: it feels like the stone has wisdom because it's been through so many generations of humans. It's

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: like bigger. It's seen it all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: Right. Also, it's also the intellectual question of intelligent design. In other words,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: when people say intelligent design, mostly it's bogus, but there are several interesting examples

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: of actual intelligent design, meaning when is a stone the product of artifice and when is it

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: a geofact produced by nature? And that was an important discovery in the 19th century,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: the zone of percussion it's called, the percussion zone. Or how do you know that a

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: signal from out of space is an intelligent signal? And as opposed to hydrogen doing something or some

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: natural thing, that's the genuine problem of intelligent design. How do you know if it's pi,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: maybe if it's E, if it's some pattern, how do you know that that's an intelligent signal?

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: How do you know that an artifact in the ground is... We'll see in the clouds a face.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: It's called pareidolia. We have a kind of a built-in ability to see faces where they really

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: aren't there. That's why kids like clowns. We've evolved that so babies evolve it to recognize

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: their parents and so forth. But when is it a projection and when is it really in the stone?

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: And that was a big question with the rise of fossils. If you find a curly thing, is that life

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: or is it non-life? People have made this mistake before. They'll find a rock on the moon or Mars,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: they say, oh, this is a face or whatever. Well, no, that's just projection. That's pareidolia.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: I guess throughout science, you have this problem of signal. Just because something is beautiful

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: doesn't mean it was... I mean, that's not a good signal to determine if it's intelligent design or

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: natural evolution or natural design. Just because you see a stone,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: that just the pattern is incredible. How do you know?

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: How do you know it's a fossil is one question, namely the remnants of an organism. And how do

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: you know if it was manipulated by a human? This is a big problem in trying to figure out the oldest

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: art. If you find scratchings on a bone, is that a tally? Is it someone marking her menstrual period?

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: Is it phases of the moon or is it trampling by an antelope? And that's called the science of

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: taphonomy to discern when a marking on a bone or a stone is in a sense an artifact or a geofact or

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: an antelope effect. And it's an intellectually challenging question. And people want to fantasize.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: They'll find a stone that looks like a carving is 300,000 years old. Generally, I think those are

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: just odd stones. You don't find the explosion of carved stone until around 60,000 years ago,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: 50,000, 60,000 years ago. There seems to be something that paleoanthropologists call the

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: creative explosion or the big bang of the mind that produces a kind of ability to see in the distance,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: to identify a shape in an object, to create a shape in an object that you don't get. The Neanderthals

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: don't seem to have ever done what we would call art. That's a very interesting phenomenon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: But it requires that you have some understanding when is something art and when is it just,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: oh, that's a rock that looks like a face. Or some not necessarily understanding,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: but a conception that's mutually agreed upon that we're able to, because maybe Neanderthals

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: maybe fish have a conception of art. They just-

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: And this also gets back to your question about professional bias and ideology, because there's

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: a huge reward for finding the oldest art. If everyone says it's 50,000 years ago and you find

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: one that's 300,000 years ago, that's a huge discovery. So there's a bias. And this has been

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: one of the things that's led to probably the overproliferation of different species of hominids,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: because there's no academic reward for finding yet another example of someone else's species.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: But there's a huge reward if you can find a Lex Friedmanite, you can name it after yourself or

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: whatever, new fossil. There's a huge professional reward to be the first at something. And so those

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: types of professional rewards also influence science and what kind of science gets done.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: Yeah. So I'm always suspicious of, and as we should all be, when you can kind of intuit

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: a financial and otherwise motivation. I mean, that's actually often in the modern age where

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: I'm suspicious of conspiracy theories. It's not that the logic doesn't make sense or something

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: like that. I personally actually just enjoy conspiracy theories. I've been listening to

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: Flat Earthers discuss stuff recently. It's kind of exciting for some reason. It's fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: Yeah. Because I consider like, what if it's true? It's exciting to discover together,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: like think through first principles, like what does the world look like? It's exciting. I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: it's the childlike discovery of a new idea. But the reason I'm skeptical of a lot of conspiracy

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: theories is when I see how popular you can get propagating those conspiracy theories,

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: how quickly you can form a large movement. And it's like, hmm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: Well, on such thin evidence, it's like if Loch Ness exists, there's just one. I mean, how does the

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: reproduction work on that? How do you talk about an animal that has only one in a population? It

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: just doesn't, some of the things don't make sense. No, but see, this is the logic side. I don't even

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: go that far. The fact is if you say there's a Loch Ness monster, I just see how quickly the idea

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: spreads in popularity. It's the people are hungry to discover something new, just like you mentioned

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: with the hominids. And I'm very suspicious of where there's like a strange hunger

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: for ideas, because then they're less likely to be objective and rigorous in considering the validity

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: of that idea. I'm not going to the logic, because actually flat earth is pretty logical.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: Yeah, very logical. Logic is not the problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: Right. But it spreads really quickly. And once again, with conspiracy theories, I think it

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: represents, you have to think about the cause of causes, the cause of the conspiracy theories.

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: Cause of causes, cause of causes, like you talked about, which is like it represents some deeper

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: fragmenting of the common humanity who have the trust in the big community that is science and

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: the big community that is government, all that kind of stuff. Yeah. Well, that's why things like

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: power, but it wasn't before 89. But still then there was a careful attention to-

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: Well, you never know how careful it was or go through the cracks or you never know when

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: something fails. You don't always know why it failed, but I was very disappointed and it ended

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

metadata.title: Podcast: Robert Proctor: Nazi Science and Ideology | Lex Fridman Podcast #268

body.input: Isaac Newton developed what we now call classical mechanics that you describe very nicely in your new book as you do with a lot of basic concepts in physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So with classical mechanics, I can throw a rock and can predict the trajectory of that rock's flight.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But if we could put ourselves back into Newton's time, his theories work to predict things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But as I understand, he himself thought that they were the interpretations of those predictions were absurd.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Perhaps he just said it for religious reasons and so on. But in particular, sort of a world of interaction without contact.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So action at a distance. It didn't make sense to him on a sort of a human interpretation level.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Does it make sense to you that things can affect other things at a distance?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It does. But, you know, that was one of Newton's worries.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You're actually right in a slightly different way about the religious worries.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: He was smart enough. This is off the topic, but still fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Newton almost invented chaos theory as soon as he invented classical mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: He realized that in the solar system, so he was able to explain how planets move around the sun.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But typically you would describe the orbit of the Earth ignoring the effects of Jupiter and Saturn and so forth, just doing the Earth and the sun.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: He kind of knew, even though he couldn't do the math, that if you included the effects of Jupiter and Saturn and the other planets, the solar system would be unstable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Like the orbits of the planets would get out of whack.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So he thought that God would intervene occasionally to sort of move the planets back into orbit, which is the only way you could explain how they were there, presumably forever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But the worries about classical mechanics were a little bit different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The worry about gravity in particular. It wasn't a worry about classical mechanics. It was a worry about gravity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: How in the world does the Earth know that there's something called the Sun 93 million miles away that is exerting gravitational force on it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And he literally said, you know, I leave that for future generations to think about because I don't know what the answer is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And in fact, people under emphasize this, but future generations figured it out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Pierre-Simon Laplace in circa 1800 showed that you could rewrite Newtonian gravity as a field theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So instead of just talking about the force due to gravity, you can talk about the gravitational field or the gravitational potential field.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And then there's no action at a distance. It's exactly the same theory empirically. It makes exactly the same predictions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But what's happening is instead of the Sun just reaching out across the void, there is a gravitational field in between the Sun and the Earth that obeys an equation, Laplace's equation, cleverly enough.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And that tells us exactly what the field does.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So even in Newtonian gravity, you don't need action at a distance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Now, what many people say is that Einstein solved this problem because he invented general relativity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And in general relativity, there's certainly a field in between the Earth and the Sun.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But also there's the speed of light as a limit. In Laplace's theory, which was exactly Newton's theory, just in a different mathematical language, there could still be instantaneous action across the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Whereas in general relativity, if you shake something here, its gravitational impulse radiates out at the speed of light.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And we call that a gravitational wave and we can detect those.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So but I really it rubs me the wrong way to think that we should presume the answer should look one way or the other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Like if it turned out that there was action at a distance in physics and that was the best way to describe things, then I would do it that way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's actually a very deep question because when we don't know what the right laws of physics are, when we're guessing at them, when we're hypothesizing at what they might be, we are often guided by our intuitions about what they should be.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I mean, Einstein famously was very guided by his intuitions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And he did not like the idea of action at a distance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We don't know whether he was right or not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But it depends on your interpretation of quantum mechanics and it depends on even how you talk about quantum mechanics within any one interpretation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So if you see every force as a field or any other interpretation of action at a distance, it's just stepping back to sort of caveman thinking.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Do you really can you really sort of understand what it means for a force to be a field that's everywhere? So if you look at gravity, what do you think about?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I think so. Is this something that you've been conditioned by society to think that to map the fact that science is extremely well predictive of something to believing that you actually understand it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Like you can intuitively, the degree that human beings can understand anything, that you actually understand it, are you just trusting the beauty and the power of the predictive power of science?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That depends on what you mean by this idea of truly understanding something, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I mean, can I truly understand Fermat's Last Theorem? It's easy to state it, but do I really appreciate what it means for incredibly large numbers, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I think yes, I think I do understand it. But if you want to just push people on well, but your intuition doesn't go to the places where Andrew Wiles needed to go to prove Fermat's Last Theorem, then I can say fine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But I still think I understand the theorem. And likewise, I think that I do have a pretty good intuitive understanding of fields pervading space-time, whether it's the gravitational field or the electromagnetic field or whatever, the Higgs field.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Of course, one's intuition gets worse and worse as you get trickier in the quantum field theory and all sorts of new phenomena that come up in quantum field theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So our intuitions aren't perfect. But I think it's also okay to say that our intuitions get trained, right? Like, you know, I have different intuitions now than I had when I was a baby. That's okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That's not an intuition is not necessarily intrinsic to who we are. We can we can train it a little bit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So that's where I'm going to bring in Noam Chomsky for a second, who thinks that our cognitive abilities are sort of evolved through time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And so they're they're biologically constrained. And so there's a clear limit as he puts it to our cognitive abilities. And it's a very harsh limit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But you actually kind of said something interesting in nature versus nurture thing here is we can train our intuitions to sort of build up the cognitive muscles to be able to understand some of these tricky concepts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So do you think there's limits to our understanding that's deeply rooted, hard coded into our biology that we can't overcome?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There could be limits to things like our ability to visualize. Okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But when someone like Ed Witten proves a theorem about, you know, 100 dimensional mathematical spaces, he's not visualizing it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: He's doing the math that doesn't stop him from understanding the result. I think and I would love to understand this better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But my rough feeling, which is not very educated, is that, you know, there's some threshold that one crosses in abstraction when one becomes kind of like a touring machine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Right. One has the ability to contain in one's brain logical, formal, symbolic structures and manipulate them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And that's a leap that we can make as human beings that that dogs and cats haven't made.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And once you get there, I'm not sure there are any limits to our ability to understand the scientific world at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Maybe there are. There's certainly ability limits on our ability to calculate things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Right. You know, people are not very good at taking cube roots of million digit numbers in their head.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But that's not an element of understanding. It's certainly not a limited principle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So, of course, as a human, you would say that doesn't feel to be limits to our understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But sort of. Have you thought that the universe is actually a lot simpler than it appears to us and we just will never be able to like it's outside of our.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: OK, so us, our cognitive abilities combined with our mathematical prowess and whatever kind of experimental simulation devices we can put together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Is there limits to that? Is it possible there's limits to that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Well, of course, it's possible that there are limits to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Is there any good reason to think that we're anywhere close to the limits is a harder question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Look, imagine asking this question 500 years ago to the world's greatest thinkers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Right. Like are we approaching the limits of our ability to understand the natural world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And by definition, there are questions about the natural world that are most interesting to us that are the ones we don't quite yet understand.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Right. So there's always we're always faced with these puzzles we don't yet know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And I don't know what they would have said 500 years ago, but they didn't even know about classical mechanics, much less quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We know that they were nowhere close to how well they could do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Right. They could do it enormously better than they were doing at the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I see no reason why the same thing isn't true for us today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So of all the worries that keep me awake at night, the human mind's inability to rationally comprehend the world is low on the list.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So one interesting philosophical point and quantum mechanics bring up is the that you talk about the distinction between the world as it is and the world as we observe it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So staying at the human level for a second, how big is the gap between what our perception system allows us to see and the world as it is outside our mind's eye sort of sort of not at the quantum mechanical level.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah. As just are these particular tools we have, which is the few senses and cognitive abilities to process those senses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Well, that last phrase, having the cognitive abilities to process them carries a lot. Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I mean, there is our sort of intuitive understanding of the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You don't need to teach people about gravity for them to know that apples fall from trees. Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That's something that we figure out pretty quickly. Object permanence, things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The three dimensionality of space, even if we don't have the mathematical language to say that, we kind of know that it's true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: On the other hand, no one opens their eyes and sees atoms. Right. Or molecules or cells for that matter. Forget about quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So, but we got there. We got to understanding that there are atoms and cells using the combination of our senses and our cognitive capacities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So adding the ability of our cognitive capacities to our senses is adding an enormous amount.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And I don't think it is a hard and fast boundary. You know, if you believe in cells, if you believe that we understand those,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: then there's no reason you believe we can't believe in quantum mechanics just as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: What to you is the most beautiful idea in physics?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Conservation of momentum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Can you elaborate? Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: If you were Aristotle, when Aristotle wrote his book on physics, he made the following very obvious point. We're on video here, right? So people can see this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So if I push the bottle, let me cover this bottle so we do not have a mess. But okay, so I push the bottle, it moves. And if I stop pushing, it stops moving.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And this is this kind of thing is repeated a large number of times all over the place. If you don't keep pushing things, they stop moving.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: This is an indisputably true fact about our everyday environment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And for Aristotle, this blew up into a whole picture of the world in which things had natures and teleologies,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: and they had places they wanted to be. And when you were pushing them, you were moving them away from where they wanted to be, and they would return and stuff like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And it took a thousand years or 1500 years for people to say, actually, if it weren't for things like dissipation and air resistance and friction and so forth,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: the natural thing is for things to move forever in a straight line, the constant velocity, right? Conservation of momentum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And that is the reason why I think that's the most beautiful idea in physics is because it shifts us from a view of nature's and teleology to a view of patterns in the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So when you were Aristotle, you needed to talk a vocabulary of why is this happening? What's the purpose of it? What's the cause, et cetera?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Because it's nature does or does not want to do that. Whereas once you believe in conservation of momentum, things just happen. They just follow the pattern.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You have Laplace's demon, ultimately, right? You give me the state of the world today, I can predict what it's going to do in the future.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I can predict where it was in the past. It's impersonal, and it's also instantaneous. It's not directed toward any future goals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's just doing what it does given the current state of the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I think even more than either classical mechanics or quantum mechanics, that is the profound deep insight that gets modern science off the ground.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You don't need natures and purposes and goals. You just need some patterns.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So it's the first moment in our understanding of the way the universe works where you branch from the intuitive physical space to kind of the space of ideas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And also the other point you said, which is conveniently, most of the interesting ideas are acting in the moment. You don't need to know the history of time or the future.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And of course, this took a long time to get there, right? I mean, the conservation of momentum itself took hundreds of years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's weird because someone would say something interesting, and then the next interesting thing would be said like 150 or 200 years later, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: They weren't even talking to each other. They were reading each other's books.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And probably the first person to directly say that in outer space, in the vacuum, a projectile would move at a constant velocity was Avicenna, Ibn Sina in the Persian Golden Age, circa 1000.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And he didn't like the idea. He used that, just like Schrodinger used Schrodinger's cat to say, surely you don't believe that, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Ibn Sina was saying, surely you don't believe there really is a vacuum because if there was a really vacuum, things could keep moving forever, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But still, he got right, the idea that there was this conservation of something impetus or mile, he would call it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And that's 500 years, 600 years before classical mechanics and Isaac Newton.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So Galileo played a big role in this, but he didn't exactly get it right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And so it just takes a long time for this to sink in because it is so against our everyday experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Do you think it was a big leap, a brave or a difficult leap of sort of math and science to be able to say that momentum is conserved?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I do. I think it's an example of human reason in action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Even Aristotle knew that his theory had issues because you could fire an arrow and it would go a long way before it stopped.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So if his theory was things just automatically stop, what's going on?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And he had this elaborate story. I don't know if you've heard this story, but the arrow would push the air in front of it away.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And the molecules of air would run around to the back of the arrow and push it again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And anyone reading this is going like, really? That's what you thought?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But it was that kind of thought experiment that ultimately got people to say, actually, no, if it weren't for the air molecules at all, the arrow would just go on by itself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And it's always this give and take between thought and experience back and forth, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Theory and experiment, we would say today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Another big question that I think comes up certainly with quantum mechanics is what's the difference between math and physics to you?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: To me, you know, very, very roughly, math is about the logical structure of all possible worlds and physics is about our actual world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And it just feels like our actual world is a gray area when you start talking about interpretations of quantum mechanics or no, I'm certainly using the word world in the broadest sense, all of reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So I think that reality is specific. I don't think that there's every possible thing going on in reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I think there are rules, whether it's the Schrodinger equation or whatever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So I think I think that there's a sensible notion of the set of all possible worlds and we live in one of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The world that we're talking about might be a multiverse, might be many worlds of quantum mechanics, might be much bigger than the world of our everyday experience, but it's still one physically contiguous world in some sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But so if you look at the overlap of math and physics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: it feels like when physics tries to reach for understanding of our world, it uses the tools of math to sort of reach beyond the limit of our current understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: What do you make of that process of sort of using math to so you start maybe with intuition or you might start with the math and then build up an intuition or but this kind of reaching into the darkness, into the mystery of the world with math?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Well, I think I would put it a little bit differently. I think we have theories, theories of the physical world, which we then extrapolate and ask, you know, what do we conclude if we take these seriously well beyond where we've actually tested them?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It is separately true that math is really, really useful when we construct physical theories.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And, you know, famously Eugene Wigner asked about the unreasonable success of mathematics and physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I think that's a little bit wrong because anything that could happen, any other theory of physics that wasn't the real world with some other world, you could always describe it mathematically.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's just that it might be a mess.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The surprising thing is not that math works, but that the math is so simple and easy that you can write it down on a t-shirt, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I mean, that's what is amazing. That's an enormous compression of information that seems to be valid in the real world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So that's an interesting fact about our world, which maybe we could hope to explain or just take as a brute fact.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I don't know. But once you have that, you know, there's this indelible relationship between math and physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But philosophically, I do want to separate them. We don't extrapolate math because there's a whole bunch of wrong math that doesn't apply to our world, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We extrapolate the physical theory that we best think explains our world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Again, an unanswerable question. Why do you think our world is so easily compressible into beautiful equations?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah. I mean, like I just hinted at, I don't know if there's an answer to that question. There could be.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: What would an answer look like?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Well, an answer could look like if you showed that there was something about our world that maximized something, you know, the mean of the simplicity and the powerfulness of the laws of physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Or, you know, maybe we're just generic, maybe in the set of all possible worlds, this is what the world would look like, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Like, I don't really know. I tend to think not. I tend to think that there is something specific and rock bottom about the facts of our world that don't have further explanation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Like the fact that the world exists at all. And furthermore, the specific laws of physics that we have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I think that in some sense, we're just going to, at some level, we're going to say, and that's how it is. And, you know, we can't explain anything more.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I don't know how, if we're anywhere close to that right now, but that seems plausible to me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And speaking of rock bottom, one of the things sort of your book kind of reminded me or revealed to me is that what's fundamental and what's emergent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It just feels like I don't even know anymore what's fundamental in physics. If there's anything, it feels like everything, especially with quantum mechanics, is revealing to us is that most interesting things that I would, as a limited human, would think are fundamental.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Fundamental can actually be explained as emergent from the more deeper laws.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I mean, we don't know, of course. We had to get that on the table. We don't know what is fundamental. We do know. We do have reason to say that certain things are more fundamental than others, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Atoms and molecules are more fundamental than cells and organs. Quantum fields are more fundamental than atoms and molecules. We don't know if that ever bottoms out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I do think that there's sensible ways to think about this. If you describe something like this table as a table, it has a height and a width, and it's made of a certain material, and it has a certain solidity and weight and so forth, that's a very useful description as far as it goes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There's a whole other description of this table in terms of a whole collection of atoms strung together in certain ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The language of the atoms is more comprehensive than the language of the table. You could break apart the table, smash it to pieces, still talk about it as atoms, but you could no longer talk about it as a table, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So I think that this comprehensiveness, the domain of validity of a theory, gets broader and broader as the theory gets more and more fundamental.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So what do you think Newton would say, maybe right in a book review, if you read your latest book on quantum mechanics, something deeply hidden?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It would take a long time for him to think that any of this was making any sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You catch him up pretty quick in the beginning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You give him a shout out in the beginning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That's right. I mean, he was the man. I'm happy to say that Newton was the greatest scientist who ever lived.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I mean, he invented calculus in his spare time, which would have made him the greatest mathematician just all by himself, right? All by that one thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But of course, you know, it's funny because Newton was in some sense still a pre-modern thinker.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Rocky Kolb, who is a cosmologist at the University of Chicago, said that Galileo, even though he came before Newton, was a more modern thinker than Newton was.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Like if you got Galileo and brought him to the present day, you take him six months to catch up and then he'd be in your office telling you why your most recent paper was wrong.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Whereas Newton just thought in this kind of more mystical way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You know, he wrote a lot more about the Bible and alchemy than he ever did about physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But he's also more brilliant than anybody else and way more mathematically astute than Galileo.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So I really don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You know, he might have he might just, yeah, say like, give me the textbooks, leave me alone for a few months and then be caught up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But he but he or he might have had mental blocks against against seeing the world in this way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I really don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Or perhaps find an interesting mystical interpretation of quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Very possible. Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Is there any other scientists or philosophers through history that you would like to know their opinion of your book?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That's a good question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I mean, Einstein is the obvious one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We all and he was not that long ago, but I even speculate at the end of my book about what his opinion would be.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I am curious as to, you know, what about older philosophers like Hume or Kant?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Right. Like, what would they have thought?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Or Aristotle, you know, what would they have thought about modern physics?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Because they do in philosophy, your predilections end up playing a much bigger role in your ultimate conclusions because you're not as tied down by what the data is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: In physics, you know, physics is lucky because we can't stray too far off the reservation as long as we're trying to explain the world that we actually see in our telescopes and microscopes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But it's just not fair to play that game because the people we're thinking about didn't know a whole bunch of things that we know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Right. Like we live through a lot that they didn't live through.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So by the time we got them caught up, they'd be different people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So let me ask a bunch of basic questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I think it would be interesting, useful for people who are not familiar, but even for people who are extremely well familiar.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Let's start with what is quantum mechanics?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Quantum mechanics is the paradigm of physics that came into being in the early part of the 20th century that replaced classical mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And it replaced classical mechanics in a weird way that we're still coming to terms with.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So in classical mechanics, you have an object, it has a location, has a velocity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And if you know the location and velocity of everything in the world, you can say what everything is going to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Quantum mechanics has an aspect of it that is kind of on the same lines.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There's something called the quantum state or the wave function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And there's an equation governing what the quantum state does.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So it's very much like classical mechanics. The wave function is different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's sort of a wave. It's a vector in a huge dimensional vector space rather than a position and a velocity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But OK, that's a detail. And the equation is the Schrodinger equation, not Newton's laws.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But OK, again, a detail. Where quantum mechanics really becomes weird and different is that there's a whole other set of rules in our textbook formulation of quantum mechanics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: in addition to saying that there's a quantum state and it evolves in time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And all these new rules have to do with what happens when you look at the system, when you observe it, when you measure it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: In classical mechanics, there were no rules about observing. You just look at it and you see what's going on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That was it, right? In quantum mechanics, the way we teach it, there's something profoundly fundamental about the act of measurement or observation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And the system dramatically changes its state, even though it has a wave function, like the electron in an atom is not orbiting in a circle, it's sort of spread out in a cloud.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: When you look at it, you don't see that cloud. When you look at it, it looks like a particle with a location.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So it dramatically changes its state right away. And the effects of that change can be instantly seen in what the electron does next.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So that's the again, we need to be careful because we don't agree on what quantum mechanics says.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So I think that's why I need to say like in the textbook view, et cetera. Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But in the textbook view, quantum mechanics, unlike any other theory of physics, places gives a fundamental role to the act of measurement.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So maybe even more basic, what is an atom and what is an electron?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Sure. This all came together, you know, in a few years around the turn of the last century, right around the year 1900.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Atoms predated then, of course, the word atom goes back to the ancient Greeks, but it was the chemists in the 1800s that really first got experimental evidence for atoms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: They realized, you know, that there were two different types of tin oxide.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And in these two different types of tin oxide, there was exactly twice as much oxygen in one type as the other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And like, why is that? Why is it why is it never 1.5 times as much? Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And so Dalton said, well, it's because there are tin atoms and oxygen atoms and one form of tin oxide is one atom of tin and one atom of oxygen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And the other is one atom of tin and two atoms of oxygen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And on the basis of this, you know, speculation, a theory, right, a hypothesis.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But then on the basis of that, you make other predictions and the chemists became quickly convinced that atoms were real.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The physicists took a lot longer to catch on, but eventually they did.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And I mean, Boltzmann, who believed in atoms, was got he had a really tough time his whole life because he worked in Germany where atoms were not popular.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: They were popular in England, but not in Germany.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And they're in general, the idea of atoms is it's the most the smallest building block of the universe for them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That's the kind of how they have a Greek idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But the chemists in the 1800s jumped the gun a little bit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So these days, an atom is the smallest building block of a chemical element, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Hydrogen, tin, oxygen, carbon, whatever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But we know that atoms can be broken up further than that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And that's what physicists discovered in the early 1900s.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Rutherford, especially, and his colleagues.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So the atom that we think about now, the cartoon, is that picture you you've always seen of a little nucleus and then electrons orbiting it like a little solar system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And we now know the nucleus is made of protons and neutrons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So the weight of the atom, the mass is almost all in its nucleus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Protons and neutrons are something like 1800 times as heavy as electrons are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Electrons are much lighter, but because they're lighter, they give all the life to the atoms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So when atoms get together, combined chemically, when electricity flows through a system, it's all the electrons that are doing all the work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And where quantum mechanics steps in, as you mentioned, with the position of velocity with classical mechanics and quantum mechanics is modeling the behavior of the electron.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I mean, you can model the behavior of anything, but the electron, because that's where the fun is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The electron was the biggest challenge right from the start.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah. So what's the wave function?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You said it's an interesting detail.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah. But in any interpretation, what is the wave function in quantum mechanics?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47
