body.input: Well, we had this idea from Rutherford that atoms look like little solar systems, but people very quickly realize that can't possibly be right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Because if an electron is orbiting in a circle, it will give off light.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: All the light that we have in this room comes from electrons zooming up and down and wiggling.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And that's what electromagnetic waves are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And you can calculate how long would it take for the electron just to spiral into the nucleus?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And the answer is 10 to the minus 11 seconds.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Okay. A hundred billionth of a second. So that's not right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Meanwhile, people had realized that light, which we understood from the 1800s was a wave, had properties that were similar to that of particles.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: This was Einstein and Planck and stuff like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So if something that we agree was a wave had particle-like properties, then maybe something we think is a particle, the electron, has wave-like properties.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And so a bunch of people eventually came to the conclusion, don't think about the electron as a little point particle orbiting like a solar system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Think of it as a wave that is spread out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: They cleverly gave this the name the wave function, which is the dopiest name in the world for one of the most profound things in the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There's literally a number at every point in space, which is the value of the electron's wave function at that point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And there's only one wave function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah. They eventually figured that out. That took longer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But when you have two electrons, you do not have a wave function for electron one and a wave function for electron two.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You have one combined wave function for both of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And indeed, as you say, there's only one wave function for the entire universe at once.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And that's where this beautiful dance, can you say what is entanglement?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It seems one of the most fundamental ideas of quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Well, let's temporarily buy into the textbook interpretation of quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And what that says is that this wave function, so it's very small outside the atom, very big in the atom.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Basically, the wave function, you take it and you square it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You square the number that gives you the probability of observing the system at that location.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So if you say that for two electrons, there's only one wave function,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: and that wave function gives you the probability of observing both electrons at once doing something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So maybe the electron can be here or here, here or here, and the other electron can also be there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But we have a wave function set up where we don't know where either electron is going to be seen,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: but we know they'll both be seen in the same place.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So we don't know exactly what we're going to see for either electron, but there's entanglement between the two of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There's a sort of conditional statement. If we see one in one location, then we know the other one's going to be doing a certain thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So that's a feature of quantum mechanics that is nowhere to be found in classical mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: In classical mechanics, there's no way I can say, well, I don't know where either one of these particles is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: but if I find out where this one is, then I know where the other one is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That just never happens. They're truly separate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And in general, it feels like if you think of a wave function like as a dance floor,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: it seems like entanglement is strongest between things that are dancing together closest.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So there's a closeness that's important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Well, that's another step. We have to be careful here because in principle,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: if you're talking about the entanglement of two electrons, for example,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: they can be totally entangled or totally unentangled no matter where they are in the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There's no relationship between the amount of entanglement and the distance between two electrons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But we now know that the reality of our best way of understanding the world is through quantum fields,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: not through particles. So even the electron, not just gravity and electromagnetism,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: but even the electron and the quarks and so forth are really vibrations in quantum fields.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So even empty space is full of vibrating quantum fields.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And those quantum fields in empty space are entangled with each other in exactly the way you just said.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: If they're nearby, if you have like two vibrating quantum fields that are nearby,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: then they will be highly entangled. If they're far away, they will not be entangled.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So what do quantum fields in a vacuum look like? Empty space?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Just like empty space. It's as empty as it can be.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But there's still a field. It's just, what does nothing look like?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Just like right here, this location in space, there's a gravitational field,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: which I can detect by dropping something. I don't see it, but there it is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So we got a little bit of idea of entanglement.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Now, what is Hilbert space and Euclidean space?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah, I think that people are very welcome to go through their lives not knowing what Hilbert space is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But if you want to dig into a little bit more into quantum mechanics, it becomes necessary.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The English language was invented long before quantum mechanics or various forms of higher mathematics were invented.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So we use the word space to mean different things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Of course, most of us think of space as this three-dimensional world in which we live.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Some of us just think of it as outer space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But space around us gives us the three-dimensional location of things and objects.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But mathematicians use any generic abstract collection of elements as a space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: A space of possibilities, momentum space, etc.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So Hilbert space is the space of all possible quantum wave functions, either for the universe or for some specific system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And it could be an infinite dimensional space or it could be just really, really large dimensional, but finite.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We don't know because we don't know the final theory of everything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But this abstract Hilbert space is really, really, really big and has no immediate connection to the three-dimensional space in which we live.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: What do dimensions in Hilbert space mean?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's just a way of mathematically representing how much information is contained in the state of the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: How many numbers do you have to give me to specify what the thing is doing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So in classical mechanics, I give you the location of something by giving you three numbers, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Up, down, left, X, Y, Z coordinates.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But then I might want to give you its entire state, physical state, which means both its position and also its velocity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The velocity also has three components.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So its state lives in something called phase space, which is six-dimensional, three dimensions of position, three dimensions of velocity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And then if it also has an orientation in space, that's another three dimensions and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So as you describe more and more information about the system, you have an abstract mathematical space that has more and more numbers that you need to give.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And each one of those numbers corresponds to a dimension in that space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So in terms of the amount of information, what is entropy?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: This mystical word that's overused in math and physics, but has a very specific meaning in this context.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Sadly, it has more than one very specific meaning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: This is the reason why it is hard.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Entropy means different things, even to different physicists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But one way of thinking about it is a measure of how much we don't know about the state of the system, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So if I have a bottle of water molecules and I know that, OK, there's a certain number of water molecules, I could weigh it, right, and figure out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I know the volume of it and I know the temperature and pressure and things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I certainly don't know the exact position and velocity of every water molecule, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So there's a certain amount of information I know, certain amount that I don't know, that is part of the complete state of the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And that's what the entropy characterizes, how much unknown information there is, the difference between what I do know about the system and its full, exact microscopic state.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So when we try to describe a quantum mechanical system, is it infinite or finite, but very large?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah, we don't know. That depends on the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You know, it's easy to mathematically write down a system that would have a potentially infinite entropy, an infinite dimensional Hilbert space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So let's go back a little bit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We said that the Hilbert space was the space in which quantum wave functions lived for different systems that will be different sizes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: They could be infinite or finite.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So that's the number of numbers, the number of pieces of information you could potentially give me about the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So the bigger Hilbert spaces, the bigger the entropy of that system could be, depending on what I know about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: If I don't know anything about it, then it has a huge entropy, right, but only up to the size of its Hilbert space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So we don't know in the real physical world whether or not this region of space that contains that water bottle has potentially an infinite entropy or just a finite entropy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We have different arguments on different sides.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So if it's infinite, how do you think about infinity?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Is this something you can, your cognitive abilities are able to process or is it just a mathematical tool?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's somewhere in between, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I mean, we can say things about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We can use mathematical tools to manipulate infinity very, very accurately.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We can define what we mean.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You know, for any number n, there's a number bigger than it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So there's no biggest number, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So there's something called the total number of all numbers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's infinite.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But it is hard to wrap your brain around that, and I think that gives people pause because we talk about infinity as if it's a number, but it has plenty of properties that real numbers don't have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You know, if you multiply infinity by two, you get infinity again, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That's a little bit different than what we're used to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Okay, but are you comfortable with the idea that in thinking of what the real world actually is, that infinity could be part of that world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Are you comfortable that a world in some dimension and some aspect?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I'm comfortable with lots of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I mean, you know, I don't want my level of comfort to affect what I think about the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You know, I'm pretty open minded about what the world could be at the fundamental level.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah, but infinity is a tricky one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's not almost a question of comfort.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's a question of, is it an overreach of our intuition?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It could be a convenient, almost like when you add a constant to an equation just because it'll help.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It just feels like it's useful to at least be able to imagine a concept, not directly, but in some kind of way that this feels like it's a description of the real world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Think of it this way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There's only three numbers that are simple.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There's zero, there's one, and there's infinity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: A number like 318 is just bizarre.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Like that, you need a lot of bits to give me what that number is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But zero and one infinity, like once you have 300 things, you might as well have infinity things, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Otherwise, you have to say when to stop making the things, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So there's a sense in which infinity is a very natural number of things to exist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I was never comfortable with infinity because it was too good to be true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Because in math, it just helps make things work out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: When things get very large, close to infinity, things seem to work out nicely.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's kind of like, because my deepest passion is probably psychology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And I'm uncomfortable how in the average, the beauty of how much we vary is lost.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: In that same kind of sense, infinity seems like a convenient way to erase the details.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But the thing about infinity is it seems to pop up whether we like it or not, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Like you're trying to be a computer scientist, you ask yourself, well, how long will it take this program to run?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And you realize, well, for some of them, the answer is infinitely long.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's not because you tried to get there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You wrote a five line computer program. It doesn't halt.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So coming back to the textbook definition of quantum mechanics, this idea that I don't think we talked about,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: can you, this one of the most interesting philosophical points, we talked at the human level, but at the physics level,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: that at least the textbook definition of quantum mechanics separates what is observed and what is real.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: One, how does that make you feel?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And two, what does it then mean to observe something?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And why is it different than what is real?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah, my personal feeling, such as it is, is that things like measurement and observers and stuff like that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: are not going to play a fundamental role in the ultimate laws of physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But my feeling that way is because so far that's where all the evidence has been pointing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I could be wrong. And there's certainly a sense in which it would be infinitely cool

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: if somehow observation or mental cogitation did play a fundamental role in the nature of reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But I don't think so. And again, I don't see any evidence for it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So I'm not spending a lot of time worrying about that possibility.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So what do you do about the fact that in the textbook interpretation of quantum mechanics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: this idea of measurement or looking at things seems to play an important role?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Well, you come up with better interpretations of quantum mechanics, and there are several alternatives.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: My favorite is the many worlds interpretation, which says two things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Number one, you, the observer, are just a quantum system like anything else.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There's nothing special about you. Don't get so proud of yourself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You're just a bunch of atoms. You have a wave function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You obey the Schrodinger equation like everything else.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And number two, when you think you're measuring something or observing something,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: what's really happening is you're becoming entangled with that thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So when you think that there's a wave function for the electron, it's all spread out,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: but you look at it and you only see it in one location.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: What's really happening is that there's still the wave function for the electron in all those locations,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: but now it's entangled with the wave function of you in the following way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There's part of the wave function that says the electron was here and you think you saw it there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The electron was there and you think you saw it there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The electron was over there and you think you saw it there, et cetera.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So and all of those different parts of the wave function, once they come into being,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: no longer talk to each other. They no longer interact or influence each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's as if they are separate worlds.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So this was the invention of Hugh Everett III, who was a graduate student at Princeton in the 1950s.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And he said, basically, look, you don't need all these extra rules about looking at things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Just listen to what the Schrodinger equation is telling you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's telling you that you have a wave function, that you become entangled,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: and that the different versions of you no longer talk to each other.

body.input: What's the difference between splitting and copying, do you think?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Like in terms of a lot of this is an interpretation that helps us sort of model the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So perhaps shouldn't be thought of as like, you know, philosophically or metaphysically.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But even at the physics level, do you see a difference between generating new copies of the world or splitting?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I think it's better to think of in quantum mechanics in many worlds, the universe splits rather than new copies

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: because people otherwise worry about things like energy conservation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And no one who understands quantum mechanics worries about energy conservation because the equation is perfectly clear.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But if all you know is that someone told you the universe duplicates,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So a pre-existing universe splitting into two skinnier universes is a better way of thinking about it.

body.input: And mathematically, it's just like, you know, if you draw an X and Y axis and you draw a vector of length one at 45 degree angle,

body.input: So to somebody who brings up a question of saying, doesn't this violate the conservation of energy?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And the answer to it is that energy is conserved.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: All of the effort goes into how best to translate what the equation unambiguously says into plain English.
