body.input: and it sort of divides up into thinner pieces, but the total amount of universe is conserved over time

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: is a reasonably good way of putting English words to the underlying mathematics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So one of my favorite things about many worlds is, I mean, I love that there's something controversial in science.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And for some reason, it makes people actually not like upset, but just get excited.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Why do you think it is a controversial idea?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So there's a lot of, it's actually one of the cleanest ways to think about quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So why do you think there's a discomfort a little bit among certain people?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Well, I draw the distinction in my book between two different kinds of simplicity in a physical theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There's simplicity in the theory itself, right, how we describe what's going on according to the theory by its own rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But then, you know, theory is just some sort of abstract mathematical formalism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You have to map it onto the world somehow, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And sometimes, like for Newtonian physics, it's pretty obvious, like, okay, here is a bottle and it has a center of mass and things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Sometimes it's a little bit harder with general relativity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Curvature of spacetime is a little bit harder to grasp.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Quantum mechanics is very hard to map what the language you're talking in of wave functions and things like that onto reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And many worlds is the version of quantum mechanics where it is hardest to map on the underlying formalism to reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So that's where the lack of simplicity comes in, not in the theory, but in how we use the theory to map onto reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And in fact, all of the work in sort of elaborating many worlds quantum mechanics is in this effort to map it on to the world that we see.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So it's perfectly legitimate to be bugged by that, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: To say like, well, no, that's just too far away from my experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I am therefore intrinsically skeptical of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Of course, you should give up on that skepticism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: If there are no alternatives and this theory always keeps working, then eventually you should overcome your skepticism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But right now there are alternatives that are that people work to make alternatives that are by their nature closer to what we observe directly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Can you describe the alternatives?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I don't think we touched on it, sort of the Copenhagen interpretation and the many worlds.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Maybe there's a difference between the ever, ever already in many worlds and many worlds as it is now, like has the idea sort of developed and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And just in general, what is the space of promising contenders?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We have democratic debates now. There's a bunch of candidates, 12 candidates, 12 candidates on stage.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: What are the quantum mechanical candidates on stage for the debate?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So if you had a debate between quantum mechanical contenders, there would be no problem getting 12 people up there on stage.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But there would still be only three frontrunners.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And right now the frontrunners would be Everett.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Hidden variable theories are another one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So the hidden variable theories say that the wave function is real, but there's something in addition to the wave function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The wave function is not everything. It's part of reality, but it's not everything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: What else is there?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We're not sure, but in the simplest version of the theory, there are literally particles.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So many worlds says that quantum systems are sometimes are wave like in some ways and particle like in another because they really, really are waves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But under certain observational circumstances, they look like particles, whereas hidden variable says they look like waves and particles because there are both waves and particles involved in the dynamics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And that's easy to do if your particles are just non relativistic Newtonian particles moving around.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: They get pushed around by the wave function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Roughly, it becomes much harder when you take quantum field theory or quantum gravity into account.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The other big contender are spontaneous collapse theories.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So in the conventional textbook interpretation, we say when you look at a quantum system, its wave function collapses and you see it in one location.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: A spontaneous collapse theory says that every particle has a chance per second of having its wave function spontaneously collapse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The chance is very small for a typical particle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It will take hundreds of millions of years before it happens even once.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But in a table or some macroscopic object, there are way more than 100 million particles and they're all entangled with each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So when one of them collapses, it brings everything else along with it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There's a slight variation of this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That's a spontaneous collapse theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There are also induced collapse theories like Roger Penrose thinks that when the gravitational difference between two parts of the wave function becomes too large, the wave function collapses automatically.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So those are basically, in my mind, the three big alternatives.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Many worlds, which is just there's a wave function and always obeys the Schrodinger equation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Hidden variables, there's a wave function that always obeys the Schrodinger equation, but there are also new variables.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Or collapse theories, which the wave function sometimes obeys the Schrodinger equation and sometimes it collapses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So you can see that the alternatives are more complicated in their formalism than many worlds is, but they are closer to our experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So just this moment of collapse, do you think of it as a wave function?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Fundamentally, sort of a probabilistic description of the world and is collapse sort of reducing that part of the world into something deterministic?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Or again, you can now describe the position and the velocity in this simple classical model.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Well, there is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Is that how you think about collapse?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There is a fourth category, is a fourth contender.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There's a Mayor Pete of quantum mechanical interpretations, which are called epistemic interpretations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And what they say is all the wave function is, is a way of making predictions for experimental outcomes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's not mapping onto an element of reality in any real sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And in fact, two different people might have two different wave functions for the same physical system because they know different things about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Right. The wave function is really just a prediction mechanism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And then the problem with those epistemic interpretations is if you say, OK, but it's predicting about what?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Like, what is the thing that is being predicted?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And I say, no, no, no. That's not what we're here for.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We're just here to tell you what the observational outcomes are going to be.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But the other the other interpretations kind of think that the wave function is real.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yes, that's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So that's an on tick interpretation of the wave function ontology being the study of what is real, what exists as opposed to an epistemic interpretation of the wave function epistemology being the study of what we know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I would actually just love to see that debate on stage.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: There was a version of it on stage at the World Science Festival a few years ago that you can look up on YouTube.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yep, it's on YouTube. OK, awesome. I'll link it and watch it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Who won? I won.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: No, I don't know. There was no vote. There was no vote.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But those there's Brian Green was the moderator and David Albert stood up for spontaneous collapse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And Shelly Goldstein was there for hidden variables and Rutger Schock was there for epistemic approaches.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Why do you I think you mentioned it, but just elaborate, why do you find many worlds so compelling?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Well, there's two reasons, actually. One is, like I said, it is the simplest, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's like the most bare bones, austere, pure version of quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And I am someone who is very willing to put a lot of work into mapping the formalism onto reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I'm less willing to complicate the formalism itself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But the other big reason is that there's something called modern physics with quantum fields and quantum gravity and holography and space time doing things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And when you take any of the other versions of quantum theory, they bring along classical baggage.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: All of the other versions of quantum mechanics prejudice or privilege some version of classical reality like locations in space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And I think that that's a barrier to doing better at understanding the theory of everything and understanding quantum gravity and the inversions of space time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Whenever if you change your theory from, you know, here's a harmonic oscillator.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Oh, there's a spin. Here's an electromagnetic field in hidden variable theories or dynamical collapse theories.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You have to start from scratch. You have to say like, well, what are the hidden variables for this theory or how does it collapse or whatever?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Whereas many worlds is plug and play. You tell me the theory and I can give you as many worlds version.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So when we have a situation like we have with gravity and space time where the classical description seems to break down in a dramatic way,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: then I think you should start from the most quantum theory that you have, which is really many worlds.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So start with the quantum theory and try to build up a model of space time, the emergence of space time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That's OK. So I thought space time was fundamental.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah, I know. So this sort of dream that Einstein had that everybody had and everybody has of, you know, the theory of everything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So how do we build up from many worlds from quantum mechanics, a model of space time, a model of gravity?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Well, yeah, I mean, let me first mention very quickly why we think it's necessary.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You know, we've had gravity in the form that Einstein bequeathed it to us for over 100 years now, like 1915 or 1916.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: He put general relativity in the final form.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So gravity is the curvature of space time and there's a field that pervades all the universe that tells us how curved space time is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And that's a fundamentally classical. That's totally classical. Right. Exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But we also have a formalism, an algorithm for taking a classical theory and quantizing it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: This is how we get quantum electrodynamics, for example. And it could be tricky.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I mean, you think you're quantizing something, so that means taking a classical theory and promoting it to a quantum mechanical theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But you can run into problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So they ran into problems and they did that with electromagnetism, namely that certain quantities were infinity

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: and you don't like infinity. Right. So Feynman and Tomonaga and Schwinger won the Nobel Prize for teaching us how to deal with the infinities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And then Ken Wilson won another Nobel Prize for saying you shouldn't have been worried about those infinities after all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But still, that was the it's always the thought that that's how you will make a good quantum theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You'll start with a classical theory and quantize it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So if we have a classical theory, general relativity, we can quantize it or we can try to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But we run into even bigger problems with gravity than we ran into with electromagnetism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And so far, those problems are insurmountable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We have not been able to get a successful theory of gravity, quantum gravity, by starting with classical general relativity and quantizing it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And there's evidence that there's a good reason why this is true, that whatever the quantum theory of gravity is, it's not a field theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's something that has weird non-local features built into it somehow that we don't understand.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We get this idea from black holes and Hawking radiation and information conservation and a whole bunch of other ideas I talk about in the book.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So if that's true, if the fundamental theory isn't even local in the sense that an ordinary quantum field theory would be,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: then we just don't know where to start in terms of getting a classical precursor and quantizing it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So the only sensible thing, or at least the next obvious sensible thing to me would be to say, OK, let's just start intrinsically quantum and work backwards, see if we can find a classical limit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So the idea of locality, the fact that locality is not fundamental to the nature of our existence,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I guess in that sense, modeling everything as a field makes sense to me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Stuff that's close by interacts, stuff that's far away doesn't.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So what's locality and why is it not fundamental? And how is that even possible?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah, I mean, locality is the answer to the question that Isaac Newton was worried about back at the beginning of our conversation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I mean, how can the Earth know what the gravitational field of the Sun is?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And the answer, as spelled out by Laplace and Einstein and others, is that there's a field in between.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And the way a field works is that what's happening to the field at this point in space only depends directly on what's happening at points right next to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But what's happening at those points depends on what's happening right next to those.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And so you can build up an influence across space through only local interactions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That's what locality means. What happens here is only affected by what's happening right next to it. That's locality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The idea of locality is built into every field theory, including general relativity as a classical theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It seems to break down when we talk about black holes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And Hawking taught us in the 1970s that black holes radiate. They give off, they will eventually evaporate away.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: They're not completely black once we take quantum mechanics into account.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And we think, we don't know for sure, but most of us think that if you make a black hole out of certain stuff,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: then like Laplace's demon taught us, you should be able to predict what that black hole will turn into if it's just obeying the Schrodinger equation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And if that's true, there are good arguments that can't happen while preserving locality at the same time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's just that the information seems to be spread out non-locally in interesting ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And people should, you talk about holography with Leonard Susskind on your Mindscape podcast.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Oh yes, I have a podcast. I didn't even mention that. This is terrible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: No, I'm going to ask you questions about that too. And I've been not shutting up about it. It's my favorite science podcast.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's not even a science podcast. It's like a, it's a scientist doing a podcast.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That's what it is. Absolutely. Yes. Yeah. Anyway.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah. So holography is this idea when you have a black hole and black hole is a region of space inside of which gravity is so strong that you can't escape.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And there's this weird feature of black holes that again is totally a thought experiment feature because we haven't gone and probed any yet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But there seems to be one way of thinking about what happens inside a black hole as seen by an observer who's falling in,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: which is actually pretty normal. Like everything looks pretty normal until you hit the singularity and you die.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But from the point of view of the outside observer, it seems like all the information that fell in is actually smeared over the horizon in a non-local way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And that's puzzling. And that's, so holography because that's a two dimensional surface that is encapsulating the whole three dimensional thing inside. Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Still trying to deal with that. Still trying to figure out how to get there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's an indication that we need to think a little bit more subtly when we quantize gravity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Because you can describe everything that's going on in three dimensional space by looking at the two dimensional projection of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah. Means that locality doesn't, is not necessary.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Well, it means it's somehow, it's only a good approximation. It's not really what's going on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: How are we supposed to feel about that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We're supposed to feel liberated. You know, space is just a good approximation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And this was always going to be true once you started quantizing gravity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So we're just beginning now to face up to the dramatic implications of quantizing gravity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Is there other weird stuff that happens to quantum mechanics in black hole?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I don't think that anything weird has happened with quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: I think weird things happen with space time. I mean, that's what it is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Like quantum mechanics is still just quantum mechanics, but our ordinary notions of space time don't really quite work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And there's a principle that goes hand in hand with holography called complementarity,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: which says that there's no one unique way to describe what's going on inside a black hole.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Different observers will have different descriptions, both of which are accurate, but sound completely incompatible with each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So it depends on how you look at it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: The word complementarity in this context is borrowed from Niels Bohr, who points out you can measure the position or you can measure the momentum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: You can't measure both at the same time in quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So a couple of questions on many worlds.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: How does many worlds help us understand our particular branch of reality?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So, OK, that's fine and good that is everything is splitting, but we're just traveling down a single branch of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So how does it help us understand our little unique branch?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: Yeah, I mean, that's a great question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But that's the point is that we didn't invent many worlds because we thought it was cool to have a whole bunch of worlds, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: We invented it because we were trying to account for what we observe here in our world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And what we observe here in our world are wave functions collapsing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: OK, we do have a position, a situation where the electron seems to be spread out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But then when we look at it, we don't see it spread out. We see it located somewhere.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So what's going on? That's the measurement problem of quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: That's what we have to face up to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So many worlds is just a proposed solution to that problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And the answer is nothing special is happening.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's still just the Schrodinger equation, but you have a wave function too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: And that's a different answer than would be given in hidden variables or dynamical collapse theories or whatever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: So the entire point of many worlds is to explain what we observe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But it tries to explain what we already have observed, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: It's not trying to be different from what we've observed because that would be something other than quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sean Carroll: Quantum Mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation | Lex Fridman Podcast #47

body.input: But the idea that there's worlds that we didn't observe that keep branching off is kind of stimulating to the imagination.

body.input: better learning algorithms, figure out how we can get access to more and more data

body.input: for those learning algorithms to extract signal from, and then accumulate that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: iceberg of knowledge.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's a beautiful picture.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's a hopeful one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think it's potentially a little bit more than just that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And this is, this is where we perhaps reach the limits of our current

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But one thing that I think that the research community hasn't really resolved

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: in a satisfactory way is how much it matters where that experience comes from.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Like, you know, do you just like download everything on the internet and cram it

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: into essentially the 21st century analog of the giant language model and see what

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: happens, or does it actually matter whether your machine physically

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: experiences the world or in the sense that it actually attempts things, observes

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the outcome of its actions and kind of augments its experience that way?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That it chooses which parts of the world it gets to interact with and observe

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and learn from.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It may be that the world is so complex that simply obtaining a large mass of

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: sort of IID samples of the world is a very difficult way to go.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But if you are actually interacting with the world and essentially performing

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: this sort of hard negative mining by attempting what you think might work,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: observing the sometimes happy and sometimes sad outcomes of that, and

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: augmenting your understanding using that experience and you're just doing this

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: continually for many years, maybe that sort of data in some sense is actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: much more favorable to obtaining a common sense understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: One reason we might think that this is true is that what we associate with common

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: sense or lack of common sense is often characterized by the ability to reason

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: about kind of counterfactual questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Like, if I were to hear this bottle of water sitting on the table, everything is

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: fine if I were to knock it over, which I'm not going to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But if I were to do that, what would happen?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And I know that nothing good would happen from that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But if I have a bad understanding of the world, I might think that that's a good

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: way for me to like, you know, gain more utility.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If I actually go about my daily life doing the things that my current

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: understanding of the world suggests will give me high utility, in some ways,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I'll get exactly the right supervision to tell me not to do those bad things and

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: to keep doing the good things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So there's a spectrum between IID, random walk through the space of data, and then

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: there's, and what we humans do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Well, I don't even know if we do it optimal, but there might be beyond.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So this open question that you raised, where do you think systems, intelligence

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: systems that would be able to deal with this world fall?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Can we do pretty well by reading all of Wikipedia, sort of randomly sampling

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: it like language models do, or do we have to be exceptionally selective and

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: intelligent about which aspects of the world we interact with?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So I think this is first an open scientific problem, and I don't have like a clear

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: answer, but I can speculate a little bit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And what I would speculate is that you don't need to be super, super careful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think it's less about like being careful to avoid the useless stuff and more about

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: making sure that you hit on the really important stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So perhaps it's okay if you spend part of your day just guided by your curiosity,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: visiting interesting regions of your state space, but it's important for you to,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: every once in a while, make sure that you really try out the solutions that your

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: current model of the world suggests might be effective and observe whether those

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: solutions are working as you expect or not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And perhaps some of that is really essential to have kind of a perpetual improvement

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: loop.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Like this perpetual improvement loop is really like, that's really the key.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: The key that's going to potentially distinguish the best current methods from

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the best methods of tomorrow, in a sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: How important do you think is exploration or total out of the box

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: thinking exploration in this space?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Does it jump to totally different domains?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So you kind of mentioned there's an optimization problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You kind of explore the specifics of a particular strategy, whatever the thing

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: you're trying to solve.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: How important is it to explore totally outside of the strategies that have been

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: working for you so far?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's your intuition there?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah, I think it's a very problem dependent kind of question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And I think that that's actually, in some ways that question gets at one of the big

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: differences between sort of the classic formulation of a reinforcement learning problem

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and some of the sort of more open-ended reformulations of that problem that have

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: been explored in recent years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So classically, reinforcement learning is framed as a problem of maximizing utility,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: like any kind of rational AI agent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And then anything you do is in service to maximizing that utility.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But a very interesting kind of way to look at, I'm not necessarily saying this is the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: best way to look at it, but an interesting alternative way to look at these problems

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: is as something where you first get to explore the world however you please, and then afterwards

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: you will be tasked with doing something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And that might suggest a somewhat different solution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So if you don't know what you're going to be tasked with doing and you just want to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: prepare yourself optimally for whatever your uncertain future holds, maybe then you will

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: choose to attain some sort of coverage, build up sort of an arsenal of cognitive tools,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: if you will, such that later on when someone tells you now your job is to fetch the coffee

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: for me, you'll be well prepared to undertake that task.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And you see that as the modern formulation of the reinforcement learning problem, as the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: more multitask, the general intelligence kind of formulation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that's one possible vision of where things might be headed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I don't think that's by any means the mainstream or standard way of doing things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And it's not like if I had to...

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But I like it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's a beautiful vision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So maybe actually take a step back.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What is the goal of robotics?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's the general problem robotics we're trying to solve?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You actually kind of painted two pictures here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: One of sort of the narrow, one of the general.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What in your view is the big problem of robotics?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Again, ridiculously philosophical high level questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that maybe there are two ways I can answer this question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: One is there's a very pragmatic problem, which is like what would make robots...

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What would sort of maximize the usefulness of robots?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And there the answer might be something like a system where...

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: A system that can perform whatever task a human user sets for it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Within the physical constraints, of course.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If you tell it to teleport to another planet, it probably can't do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But if you ask it to do something that's within its physical capability,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: then potentially with a little bit of additional training or a little bit of additional trial

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and error, it ought to be able to figure it out in much the same way as like a human teleoperator

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: ought to figure out how to drive the robot to do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's kind of the very pragmatic view of what it would take to kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: solve the robotics problem, if you will.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But I think that there is a second answer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And that answer is a lot closer to why I want to work on robotics, which is that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think it's less about what it would take to do a really good job in the world of robotics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: but more the other way around.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What robotics can bring to the table to help us understand artificial intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So your dream fundamentally is to understand intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that's the dream for many people who actually work in this space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that there's something very pragmatic and very useful about studying robotics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But I do think that a lot of people that go into this field, actually,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the things that they draw inspiration from are the potential for robots to help us learn

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: about intelligence and about ourselves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's fascinating that robotics is basically the space by which you can get closer to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: understanding the fundamentals of artificial intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So what is it about robotics that's different from some of the other approaches?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So if we look at some of the early breakthroughs in deep learning or in the computer vision

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: space and the natural language processing, there's really nice clean benchmarks that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: a lot of people competed on and thereby came up with a lot of brilliant ideas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's the fundamental difference between computer vision purely defined and ImageNet

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and kind of the bigger robotics problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So there are a couple of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: One is that with robotics, you kind of have to take away many of the crutches.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So you have to deal with both the particular problems of perception, control, and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But you also have to deal with the integration of those things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Classically, we've always thought of the integration as kind of a separate problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So a classic kind of modular engineering approach is that we solve the individual

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: sub-problems, then wire them together, and then the whole thing works.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And one of the things that we've been seeing over the last couple of decades is that, well,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: maybe studying the thing as a whole might lead to just very different solutions than

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: if we were to study the parts and wire them together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So the integrative nature of robotics research helps us see the different perspectives on

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Another part of the answer is that with robotics, it casts a certain paradox into very clever

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: relief.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So this is sometimes referred to as a Moravix paradox, the idea that in artificial intelligence,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: things that are very hard for people can be very easy for machines, and vice versa, things

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that are very easy for people can be very hard for machines.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So integral and differential calculus is pretty difficult to learn for people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But if you program a computer, do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It can derive derivatives and integrals for you all day long without any trouble.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Whereas some things like drinking from a cup of water, very easy for a person to do, very

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: hard for a robot to deal with.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And sometimes when we see such blatant discrepancies, they give us a really strong hint that we're

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: missing something important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So if we really try to zero in on those discrepancies, we might find that little bit that we're missing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And it's not that we need to make machines better or worse at math and better at drinking

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: water, but just that by studying those discrepancies, we might find some things that we might be

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: missing, and we might find some new insight.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So that could be in any space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It doesn't have to be robotics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But you're saying, it's kind of interesting that robotics seems to have a lot of those

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: discrepancies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So the Hans-Marvá paradox is probably referring to the space of the physical interaction,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: like you said, object manipulation, walking, all the kind of stuff we do in the physical

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: How do you make sense if you were to try to disentangle the Marvá paradox?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Why is there such a gap in our intuition about it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Why do you think manipulating objects is so hard from everything you've learned from applying

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: reinforcement learning in this space?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that one reason is maybe that for many of the other problems that we've studied

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: in AI and computer science and so on, the notion of input, output, and supervision is

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: much, much cleaner.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So computer vision, for example, deals with very complex inputs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But it's comparatively a bit easier, at least up to some level of abstraction, to cast it

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: as a very tightly supervised problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's comparatively much, much harder to cast robotic manipulation as a very tightly

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: supervised problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You can do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It just doesn't seem to work all that well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So you could say that, well, maybe we get a label data set where we know exactly which

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: motor commands to send, and then we train on that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But for various reasons, that's not actually such a great solution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And it also doesn't seem to be even remotely similar to how people and animals learn to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: do things, because we're not told by our parents, here's how you fire your muscles

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: in order to walk.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: We do get some guidance, but the really low-level detailed stuff we figure out mostly on our

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: own.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And that's what you mean by tightly coupled, that every single little sub-action gets a

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: supervised signal of whether it's a good one or not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So while in computer vision, you could sort of imagine up to a level of abstraction that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: maybe somebody told you this is a car, and this is a cat, and this is a dog.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: In motor control, it's very clear that that was not the case.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If we look at sort of the sub-spaces of robotics that, again, as you said, robotics integrates

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: all of them together, and we get to see how this beautiful mess interplays.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But there's nevertheless still perception.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So it's the computer vision problem, broadly speaking, understanding the environment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Then there's also, maybe you can correct me on this kind of categorization of the space,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: then there's prediction in trying to anticipate what things are going to do into the future

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: in order for you to be able to act in that world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108
