body.input: And then there's also this game theoretic aspect of how your actions will change the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: behavior of others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: In this kind of space, and this is bigger than reinforcement learning, this is just

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: broadly looking at the problem of robotics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's the hardest problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Or is what you said true that when you start to look at all of them together, that's a

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: whole other thing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You can't even say which one individually is harder because all of them together, you

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: should only be looking at them all together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think when you look at them all together, some things actually become easier.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And I think that's actually pretty important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So we had, back in 2014, we had some work, basically our first work on end-to-end reinforcement

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning for robotic manipulation skills from vision, which at the time was something that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: seemed a little inflammatory and controversial in the robotics world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But other than the inflammatory and controversial part of it, the point that we were actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: trying to make in that work is that for the particular case of the robotics world, the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: for the particular case of combining perception and control, you could actually do better if

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: you treat them together than if you try to separate them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And the way that we tried to demonstrate this is we picked a fairly simple motor control

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: task where a robot had to insert a little red trapezoid into a trapezoidal hole.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And we had our separated solution, which involved first detecting the hole using a

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: post detector and then actuating the arm to put it in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And then our intense solution, which just mapped pixels to the torques.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And one of the things we observed is that if you use the intense solution, essentially

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the pressure on the perception part of the model is actually lower.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Like it doesn't have to figure out exactly where the thing is in 3D space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It just needs to figure out where it is, you know, distributing the errors in such a way

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that the horizontal difference matters more than the vertical difference, because vertically

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: it just pushes it down all the way until it can't go any further.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And there, perceptual errors are a lot less harmful, whereas perpendicular to the direction

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of motion, perceptual errors are much more harmful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So the point is that if you combine these two things, you can trade off errors between

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the components optimally to best accomplish the task and the components can actually be

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: weaker while still leading to better overall performance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It has a profound idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I mean, in the space of pegs and things like that, it's quite simple.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It almost is tempting to overlook, but that seems to be at least intuitively an idea that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: should generalize to basically all aspects of perception and control.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Of course.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That one strengthens the other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And we, you know, people who have studied sort of perceptual heuristics in humans and animals

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: find things like that all the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So one very well-known example of this is something called the gaze heuristic, which

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: is a little trick that you can use to intercept a flying object.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So if you want to catch a ball, for instance, you could try to localize it in 3D space,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: estimate its velocity, estimate the effect of wind resistance, solve a complex system

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of differential equations in your head, or you can maintain a running speed so that the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: object stays in the same position as in your field of view.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So if it dips a little bit, you speed up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If it rises a little bit, you slow down.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And if you follow the simple rule, you'll actually arrive at exactly the place where

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the object lands and you'll catch it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And humans use it when they play baseball.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Human pilots use it when they fly airplanes to figure out if they're about to collide

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: with somebody.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Frogs use this to catch insects and so on and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So this is something that actually happens in nature.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And I'm sure this is just one instance of it that we were able to identify just because

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: all the scientists were able to identify because it's so prevalent, but there are probably

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: many others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Just so we can zoom in as we talk about robotics, do you have a canonical problem, sort of a

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: simple, clean, beautiful, representative problem in robotics that you think about when

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: you're thinking about some of these problems?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: We talked about robotic manipulation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: To me, that seems intuitively, at least the robotics community has converged towards

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that as a space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's the canonical problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If you agree, then maybe do you zoom in in some particular aspect of that problem that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: you just like?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Like if we solve that problem perfectly, it'll unlock a major step in towards human level

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I don't think I have a really great answer to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And I think partly the reason I don't have a great answer, it has to do with the fact

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that the difficulty is really in the flexibility and adaptability rather than in doing a particular

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: thing really, really well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's hard to just say, oh, if you can shuffle a deck of cards as fast as a Vegas casino

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: dealer, then you'll be very proficient.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's really the ability to quickly figure out how to do some arbitrary new thing well

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: enough to move on to the next arbitrary thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But the source of newness and uncertainty, have you found problems in which it's easy

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: to generate new newnessnessnesses?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: New types of newness.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So a few years ago, so if you had asked me this question around like 2016 maybe, I would

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: have probably said that robotic grasping is a really great example of that because it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: a task with great real world utility.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Like you will get a lot of money if you can do it well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What is robotic grasping?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Picking up any object.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: With a robotic hand.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So you will get a lot of money if you do it well because lots of people want to run warehouses

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: with robots and it's highly non-trivial because very different objects will require very different

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: grasping strategies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But actually since then, people have gotten really good at building systems to solve this

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: problem to the point where I'm not actually sure how much more progress we can make with

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that as like the main guiding thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But it's kind of interesting to see the kind of methods that have actually worked well

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: in that space because robotic grasping classically used to be regarded very much as kind of almost

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: like a geometry problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So people who have studied the history of computer vision will find this very familiar

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that it's kind of in the same way that in the early days of computer vision, people

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: thought of it very much as like an inverse graphics thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: In robotic grasping, people thought of it as an inverse physics problem essentially.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You look at what's in front of you, figure out the shapes, then use your best estimate

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of the laws of physics to figure out where to put your fingers and then you pick up the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And it turns out that what works really well for robotic grasping instantiated in many

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: different recent works including our own but also ones from many other labs is to use learning

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: methods with some combination of either exhaustive simulation or like actual real world trial

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and error.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And it turns out that those things actually work really well and then you don't have to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: worry about solving geometry problems or physics problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So what are, just by the way in the grasping, what are the difficulties that have been worked

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: on?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So one is like the materials of things, maybe occlusions on the perception side.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Why is it such a difficult, why is picking stuff up such a difficult problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah, it's a difficult problem because the number of things that you might have to deal

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: with or the variety of things that you have to deal with is extremely large.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And oftentimes things that work for one class of objects won't work for other classes of

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: objects.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So if you get really good at picking up boxes and now you have to pick up plastic bags,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: you just need to employ a very different strategy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And there are many properties of objects that are more than just their geometry.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It has to do with the bits that are easier to pick up, the bits that are harder to pick

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: up, the bits that are more flexible, the bits that will cause the thing to pivot and bend

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and drop out of your hand versus the bits that result in a nice secure grasp, things

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that are flexible, things that if you pick them up the wrong way, they'll fall upside

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: down and the contents will spill out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So there's all these little details that come up, but the task is still kind of can be characterized

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: as one task.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Like there's a very clear notion of you did it or you didn't do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So in terms of spilling things, there creeps in this notion that starts to sound and feel

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: like common sense reasoning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Do you think solving the general problem of robotics requires common sense reasoning,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: requires general intelligence, this kind of human level capability of, like you said,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: be robust and deal with uncertainty, but also be able to sort of reason and assimilate different

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: pieces of knowledge that you have?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What are your thoughts on the needs?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's of common sense reasoning in the space of the general robotics problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So I'm going to slightly dodge that question and say that I think maybe actually it's the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: other way around is that studying robotics can help us understand how to put common sense

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: into our AI systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: One way to think about common sense and why our current systems might lack common sense

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: is that common sense is an emergent property of actually having to interact with a particular

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: world, a particular universe, and get things done in that universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So you might think that, for instance, like an image captioning system, maybe it looks

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: at pictures of the world and it types out English sentences.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So it kind of deals with our world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And then you can easily construct situations where image captioning systems do things that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: defy common sense, like give it a picture of a person wearing a fur coat and we'll say

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: it's a teddy bear.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But I think what's really happening in those settings is that the system doesn't actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: live in our world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It lives in its own world that consists of pixels and English sentences and doesn't actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: consist of having to put on a fur coat in the winter so you don't get cold.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So perhaps the reason for the disconnect is that the systems that we have now simply inhabit

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: a different universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And if we build AI systems that are forced to deal with all of the messiness and complexity

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of our universe, maybe they will have to acquire common sense to essentially maximize their

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: utility.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Whereas the systems we're building now don't have to do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: They can take some shortcuts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You've a couple of times already sort of reframed the role of robotics in this whole thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And for some reason, I don't know if my way of thinking is common, but I thought like

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: we need to understand and solve intelligence in order to solve robotics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And you're kind of framing it as no, robotics is one of the best ways to just study artificial

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: intelligence and build sort of like robotics is like the right space in which you get to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: explore some of the fundamental learning mechanisms, fundamental sort of multimodal multitask aggregation

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of knowledge mechanisms that are required for general intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's really interesting way to think about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But let me ask about learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Can the general sort of robotics, the epitome of the robotics problem be solved purely through

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning perhaps and to unlearning sort of learning from scratch as opposed to injecting

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: human expertise and rules and heuristics and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that in terms of the spirit of the question, I would say yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I mean, I think that though in some ways it's maybe like an overly sharp dichotomy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that in some ways when we build algorithms, at some point a person does something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah, hyper parameters.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: There's always a person turned on the computer, a person implemented TensorFlow.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But yeah, I think that in terms of the point that you're getting at, I do think the answer

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: is yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that we can solve many problems that have previously required meticulous manual

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: engineering through automated optimization techniques.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And actually one thing I will say on this topic is I don't think this is actually a

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: very radical or very new idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think people have been thinking about automated optimization techniques as a way to do control

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: for a very, very long time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And in some ways what's changed is really more the name.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So today we would say that, oh, my robot does machine learning, it does reinforcement learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Maybe in the 1960s you'd say, oh, my robot is doing optimal control.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And maybe the difference between typing out a system of differential equations and doing

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: feedback linearization versus training a neural net, maybe it's not such a large difference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's just pushing the optimization deeper and deeper into the thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Well, it's interesting you think that way, but especially with deep learning that the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: accumulation of experiences in data form to form deep representations starts to feel like

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: knowledge as opposed to optimal control.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So this feels like there's an accumulation of knowledge through the learning process.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So I think that is a good point that one big difference between learning-based systems

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and classic optimal control systems is that learning-based systems in principle should

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: get better and better the more they do something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And I do think that that's actually a very, very powerful difference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So if we look back at the world of expert systems, the symbolic AI and so on, of using

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: logic to accumulate expertise, human expertise, human encoded expertise, do you think that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: will have a role at some point?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Deep learning, machine learning, reinforcement learning has shown incredible results and

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: breakthroughs and just inspired thousands, maybe millions of researchers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But there's this less popular now, but it used to be popular idea of symbolic AI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Do you think that will have a role?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think in some ways the descendants of symbolic AI actually already have a role.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So this is the highly biased history from my perspective.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You say that, well, initially we thought that rational decision making involves logical

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: manipulation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So you have some model of the world expressed in terms of logic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You have some query like what action do I take in order for X to be true?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And then you manipulate your logical symbolic representation to get an answer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What that turned into somewhere in the 1990s is, well, instead of building predicates and

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: statements that have true or false values, we'll build probabilistic systems where things

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: have probabilities associated and probabilities of being true and false.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And that turned into Bayes nets.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And that provided a boost to what were really still essentially logical inference systems,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: just probabilistic logical inference systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And then people said, well, let's actually learn the individual probabilities inside

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: these models.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And then people said, well, let's not even specify the nodes in the models.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Let's just put a big neural net in there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But in many ways, I see these as actually kind of descendants from the same idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's essentially instantiating rational decision making by means of some inference process

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and learning by means of an optimization process.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So in a sense, I would say, yes, that it has a place.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And in many ways, that place is already holds that place.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's already in there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah, it's just by different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It looks slightly different than it was before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But there are things that we can think about that make this a little bit more obvious.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If I train a big neural net model to predict what will happen in response to my robot's

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: actions, and then I run probabilistic inference, meaning I invert that model to figure out

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the actions that lead to some plausible outcome, to me, that seems like a kind of logic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You have a model of the world that just happens to be expressed by a neural net.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And you are doing some inference procedure, some sort of manipulation on that model to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: figure out the answer to a query that you have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's the interpretability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's the explainability, though, that seems to be lacking more so, because the nice thing

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: about expert systems is you can follow the reasoning of the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: To us, mere humans is somehow compelling.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's just I don't know what to make of this fact that there's a human desire for intelligent

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: systems to be able to convey in a poetic way to us why it made the decisions it did.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Tell a convincing story.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Perhaps that's a silly human thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: We shouldn't expect that of intelligent systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: We should be super happy that there is intelligent systems out there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But if I were to psychoanalyze the researchers at the time, I would say expert systems can

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: be connected to that part, that desire of AI researchers for systems to be explainable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Maybe on that topic, do you have a hope that inference systems, learning-based systems

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: will be as explainable as the dream was with expert systems, for example?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think it's a very complicated question, because I think that in some ways the question

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of explainability is very closely tied to the question of performance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Why do you want your system to explain itself?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So that when it screws up, you can figure out why it did it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But in some ways, that's a much bigger problem, actually.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Your system might screw up, and then it might screw up in how it explains itself, or you

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: might have some bug somewhere so that it's not actually doing what it was supposed to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Maybe a good way to view that problem is really as a bigger problem of verification and validation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of which explainability is one component.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I see.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I just see it differently.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I see explainability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You put it beautifully.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think you actually summarized the field of explainability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But to me, there's another aspect of explainability, which is storytelling, that has nothing to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: do with errors or with...

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It uses errors as elements of its story, as opposed to a fundamental need to be explainable

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: when errors occur.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's just that for other intelligent systems to be in our world, we seem to want to tell

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: each other stories.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's true in the political world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's true in the academic world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Political networks are less capable of doing that, or perhaps they're equally capable of

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: storytelling storytelling.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Maybe it doesn't matter what the fundamentals of the system are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You just need to be a good storyteller.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Maybe one specific story I can tell you about in that space is actually about some work

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that was done by my former collaborator, who's now a professor at MIT named Jacob Andreas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Jacob actually works in natural language processing, but he had this idea to do a little bit of

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: work in reinforcement learning on how natural language can basically structure the internals

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of policies trained with RL.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: One of the things he did is he set up a model that attempts to perform some task that's

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: defined by a reward function, but the model reads in a natural language instruction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: This is a pretty common thing to do in instruction following.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You tell it, go to the red house, and then it's supposed to go to the red house.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But then one of the things that Jacob did is he treated that sentence not as a command

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: from a person, but as a representation of the internal state of the mind of this policy,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: essentially, so that when it was faced with a new task, what it would do is it would basically

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: try to think of possible language descriptions, attempt to do them, and see if they led to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the right outcome.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It would think out loud.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I'm faced with this new task.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What am I going to do?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Let me go to the red house.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Oh, that didn't work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Let me go to the blue room or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Let me go to the green plant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Once it got some reward, it would say, oh, go to the green plant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's what's working.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I'm going to go to the green plant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Then you could look at the string that it came up with, and that was a description of

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: how it thought it should solve the problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You could basically incorporate language as internal state, and you can start getting

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: some handle on these kinds of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Then what I was trying to get to is that also if you add to the reward function the convincingness

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of that story.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I have another reward signal of people who review that story, how much they like it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Initially that could be a hyperparameter, hard-coded, heuristic type of thing, but it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: an interesting notion of the convincingness of the story becoming part of the reward function,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the objective function of the explainability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: In the world of Twitter and fake news, that might be a scary notion that the nature of

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: truth may not be as important as the convincingness of how convincing you are in telling the story

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: around the facts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Let me ask the basic question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You're one of the world-class researchers in reinforcement learning, deep reinforcement

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning, certainly in the robotics space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What is reinforcement learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that what reinforcement learning refers to today is really just the modern incarnation

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of learning-based control.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Classically reinforcement learning has a much more narrow definition, which is that it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: literally learning from reinforcement, like the thing does something and then it gets

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: a reward or punishment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But really I think the way the term is used today is it's used to refer more broadly to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning-based control.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Some kind of system that's supposed to be controlling something and it uses data to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: get better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What does control mean?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So, it's action is the fundamental element there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It means making rational decisions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Rational decisions are decisions that maximize a measure of utility.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And sequentially, so you make decisions time and time and time again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's easier to see that kind of idea in the space of maybe games and the space of robotics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Do you see it bigger than that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Is it applicable?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What are the limits of the applicability of reinforcement learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So, rational decision-making is essentially the encapsulation of the AI problem viewed

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: in through a particular lens.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So any problem that we would want a machine to do, an intelligent machine can likely be

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: represented as a decision-making problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Classifying images is a decision-making problem, although not a sequential one typically.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Using a chemical plant as a decision-making problem, deciding what videos to recommend

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: on YouTube is a decision-making problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And one of the really appealing things about reinforcement learning is if it does encapsulate

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the range of all these decision-making problems, perhaps working on reinforcement learning

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: is one of the ways to reach a very broad swath of AI problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But what do you use the fundamental difference between reinforcement learning and maybe supervised

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: machine learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So reinforcement learning can be viewed as a generalization of supervised machine learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You can certainly cast supervised learning as a reinforcement learning problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You can just say your loss function is the negative of your reward, but you have stronger

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: assumptions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You have the assumption that someone actually told you what the correct answer was, that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: your data was IID and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So you could view reinforcement learning as essentially relaxing some of those assumptions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Now, that's not always a very productive way to look at it because if you actually have

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: a supervised learning problem, you'll probably solve it much more effectively by using supervised

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning methods because it's easier.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But you can view reinforcement learning as a generalization of that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: No, for sure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But they're fundamentally different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's a mathematical statement that's absolutely correct.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But it seems that reinforcement learning, the kind of tools we'll bring to the table

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: today of today, so maybe down the line, everything will be a reinforcement learning problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Just like you said, image classification should be mapped to a reinforcement learning problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But today, the tools and ideas, the way we think about them are different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Supervised learning has been used very effectively to solve basic narrow AI problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Reinforcement learning kind of represents the dream of AI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's very much so in the research space now in sort of captivating the imagination of

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: people of what we can do with intelligent systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But it hasn't yet had as wide of an impact as the supervised learning approaches.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: My question comes from the more practical sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What do you see is the gap between the more general reinforcement learning and the very

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: specific, yes, it's sequential decision making with one step in the sequence of the supervised

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So from a practical standpoint, I think that one thing that is potentially a little tough

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: now, and this is I think something that we'll see, this is a gap that we might see closing

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: over the next couple of years, is the ability of reinforcement learning algorithms to effectively

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: utilize large amounts of prior data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So one of the reasons why it's a bit difficult today to use reinforcement learning for all

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the things that we might want to use it for is that in most of the settings where we want

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: to do rational decision making, it's a little bit tough to just deploy some policy that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: does crazy stuff and learns purely through trial and error.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's much easier to collect a lot of data, a lot of logs of some other policy that you've

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: got and then maybe if you can get a good policy out of that, then you deploy it and let it

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: kind of fine tune a little bit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But algorithmically, it's quite difficult to do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So I think that once we figure out how to get reinforcement learning to bootstrap effectively

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: from large data sets, then we'll see very, very rapid growth in applications of these

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: technologies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So this is what's referred to as off-policy reinforcement learning or offline RL or batch

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: RL.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And I think we're seeing a lot of research right now that's bringing us closer and closer

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Can you maybe paint the picture of the different methods?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You said off-policy, what's value-based reinforcement learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's policy-based?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's model-based?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's off-policy on policy?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What are the different categories of reinforcement learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So, one way we can think about reinforcement learning is that it's in some very fundamental

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: way, it's about learning models that can answer kind of what-if questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So what would happen if I take this action that I hadn't taken before?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And you do that, of course, from experience, from data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And oftentimes, you do it in a loop.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So you build a model that answers these what-if questions, use it to figure out the best action

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: you can take, and then go and try taking that and see if the outcome agrees with what you

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: predicted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So the different kinds of techniques basically refer to different ways of doing it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So model-based methods answer a question of what state you would get, basically what would

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: happen to the world if you were to take a certain action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Value-based methods, they answer the question of what value you would get, meaning what

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: utility you would get.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But in a sense, they're not really all that different because they're both really just

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: answering these what-if questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Now unfortunately for us, with current machine learning methods, answering what-if questions

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: can be really hard because they are really questions about things that didn't happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If you wanted to answer what-if questions about things that did happen, you wouldn't

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: need a learned model.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You would just repeat the thing that worked before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And that's really a big part of why RL is a little bit tough.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So if you have a purely on-policy kind of online process, then you ask these what-if

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: questions, you make some mistakes, then you go and try doing those mistaken things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And then you observe kind of the counter examples that will teach you not to do those things

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If you have a bunch of off-policy data and you just want to synthesize the best policy

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: you can out of that data, then you really have to deal with the challenges of making

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: these counterfactual.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: First of all, what's a policy?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: A policy is a model or some kind of function that maps from observations of the world to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: actions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So in reinforcement learning, we often refer to the current configuration of the world

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: as the state.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So we say the state kind of encompasses everything you need to fully define where the world is

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: at at the moment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And depending on how we formulate the problem, we might say you either get to see the state

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: or you get to see an observation, which is some snapshot, some piece of the state.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So policy just includes everything in it in order to be able to act in this world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And so what does off-policy mean?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So the terms on-policy and off-policy refer to how you get your data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So if you get your data from somebody else who was doing some other stuff, maybe you

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: get your data from some manually programmed system that was just running in the world

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: before that's referred to as off-policy data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But if you got the data by actually acting in the world based on what your current policy

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: thinks is good, we call that on-policy data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108
