body.input: And obviously, on-policy data is more useful to you because if your current policy makes

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: some bad decisions, you will actually see that those decisions are bad.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Off-policy data, however, might be much easier to obtain because maybe that's all the log

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of data that you have from before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So we talked about offline, talked about autonomous vehicles so you can envision off-policy kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of approaches in robotic spaces where there's already a ton of robots out there, but they

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: don't get the luxury of being able to explore based on a reinforcement learning framework.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So how do we make, again, open question, but how do we make off-policy methods work?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So this is something that has been kind of a big open problem for a while.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And in the last few years, people have made a little bit of progress on that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I can tell you about, and it's not by any means solved yet, but I can tell you some

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of the things that, for example, we've done to try to address some of the challenges.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It turns out that one really big challenge with off-policy reinforcement learning is

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that you can't really trust your models to give accurate predictions for any possible

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: action.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So if I've never tried to, if in my data set I never saw somebody steering the car off

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the road onto the sidewalk, my value function or my model is probably not going to predict

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the right thing if I ask what would happen if I were to steer the car off the road onto

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the sidewalk.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So one of the important things you have to do to get off-policy RL to work is you have

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: to be able to figure out whether a given action will result in a trustworthy prediction or

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And you can use kind of distribution estimation methods, kind of density estimation methods

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: to try to figure that out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So you could figure out that, well, this action, my model is telling me that it's great, but

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: it looks totally different from any action I've taken before, so my model is probably

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: not correct.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And you can incorporate regularization terms into your learning objective that will essentially

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: tell you not to ask those questions that your model is unable to answer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What would lead to breakthroughs in this space, do you think?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's needed?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Is this a data set question?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Do we need to collect big benchmark data sets that allow us to explore the space?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Is it new kinds of methodologies?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's your sense?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Or maybe coming together in a space of robotics and defining the right problem to be working

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: on?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think for off-policy reinforcement learning in particular, it's very much an algorithms

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: question right now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And this is something that I think is great because an algorithms question is that that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: just takes some very smart people to get together and think about it really hard.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Whereas if it was like a data problem or hardware problem, that would take some serious engineering.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So that's why I'm pretty excited about that problem because I think that we're in a position

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: where we can make some real progress on it just by coming up with the right algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: In terms of which algorithms they could be, the problems at their core are very related

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: to problems in things like causal inference, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Because what you're really dealing with is situations where you have a model, a statistical

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: model that's trying to make predictions about things that I hadn't seen before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And if it's a model that's generalizing properly, that'll make good predictions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If it's a model that picks up on spurious correlations that will not generalize properly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And then you have an arsenal of tools you can use.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You could, for example, figure out what are the regions where it's trustworthy or on the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: other hand, you could try to make it generalize better somehow or some combination of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: two.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Is there room for mixing sort of where most of it like 90, 95% is off policy, you already

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: have the data set and then you get to send the robot out to do a little exploration.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Like what's that role of mixing them together?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah, absolutely.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that this is something that you actually described very well at the beginning of our

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: discussion when you talked about the iceberg.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: This is the iceberg, that the 99% of your prior experience, that's your iceberg.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You'd use that for off policy reinforcement learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And then of course, if you've never opened that particular kind of door with that particular

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: lock before, then you have to go out and fiddle with it a little bit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And that's that additional 1% to help you figure out a new task.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And I think that's actually like a pretty good recipe going forward.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Is this to you the most exciting space of reinforcement learning now?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Or is there, what's, and maybe taking a step back, not just now, but what's to you is the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: most beautiful idea?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Apologize for the romanticized question, but the beautiful idea or concept in reinforcement

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: In general, I actually think that one of the things that is a very beautiful idea in reinforcement

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning is just the idea that you can obtain a near optimal controller, a near optimal

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: policy without actually having a complete model of the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's something that feels perhaps kind of obvious if you just hear the term reinforcement

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning or you think about trial and error learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But from a controls perspective, it's a very weird thing because classically, we think

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: about engineered systems and controlling engineered systems as the problem of writing down some

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: equations and then figuring out, given these equations, basically solve for X, figure out

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the thing that maximizes its performance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And the theory of reinforcement learning actually gives us a mathematically principled framework

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: to think, to reason about optimizing some quantity when you don't actually know the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: equations that govern that system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And to me, that actually seems very elegant, not something that becomes immediately obvious,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: at least in the mathematical sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Does it make sense to you that it works at all?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Well, I think it makes sense when you take some time to think about it, but it is a little

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: surprising.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Well, then taking a step into the more deeper representations, which is also very surprising,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the richness of the state space, the space of environments that this kind of approach

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: can operate in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Can you maybe say, what is deep reinforcement learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Well, deep reinforcement learning simply refers to taking reinforcement learning algorithms

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and combining them with high capacity neural net representations, which is kind of, it

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: might at first seem like a pretty arbitrary thing, just take these two components and

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: stick them together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But the reason that it's something that has become so important in recent years is that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: reinforcement learning, it kind of faces an exacerbated version of a problem that has

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: faced many other machine learning techniques.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So if we go back to the early 2000s or the late 90s, we'll see a lot of research on machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning methods that have some very appealing mathematical properties, like they reduced

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the convex optimization problems, for instance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But they require very special inputs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: They require a representation of the input that is clean in some way, like for example,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: clean in the sense that the classes in your multi-class classification problems separate

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: linearly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So it's some kind of good representation, and we call this feature representation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And for a long time, people were very worried about features in the world of supervised

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning because somebody had to actually build those features.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So you couldn't just take an image and plug it into your logistic regression or your SVM

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Someone had to take that image and process it using some handwritten code.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And then neural nets came along and they could actually learn the features.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And suddenly we could apply learning directly to the raw inputs, which was great for images,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: but it was even more great for all the other fields where people hadn't come up with good

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: features yet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And one of those fields was actually reinforcement learning, because in reinforcement learning,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the notion of features, if you don't use neural nets and you have to design your own features,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: is very, very opaque.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's very hard to imagine, let's say I'm playing chess or Go.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What is a feature with which I can represent the value function for Go or even the optimal

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: policy for Go linearly?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I don't even know how to start thinking about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And people tried all sorts of things that would write down, an expert chess player looks

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: for whether the knight is in the middle of the board or not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So that's a feature, is knight in middle of board?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And they would write these long lists of arbitrary made up stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And that was really getting us nowhere.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And chess is a little more accessible than the robotics problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Absolutely.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: There's at least experts in the different features for chess.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But still like the neural network there, to me, that's, I mean, you put it eloquently

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and almost made it seem like a natural step to add neural networks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But the fact that neural networks are able to discover features in the control problem,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: it's very interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's hopeful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I'm not sure what to think about it, but it feels hopeful that the control problem has

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: features to be learned.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Like I guess my question is, is it surprising to you how far the deep side of deep reinforcement

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning was able to, like what the space of problems has been able to tackle from,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: especially in games with the Alpha Star and Alpha Zero and just the representation power

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: there and in the robotics space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And what is your sense of the limits of this representation power and the control context?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that in regard to the limits that here, I think that one thing that makes it

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: a little hard to fully answer this question is because in settings where we would like

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: to push these things to the limit, we encounter other bottlenecks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So the reason that I can't get my robot to learn how to do the dishes in the kitchen,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: it's not because its neural net is not big enough.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's because when you try to actually do trial and error learning, reinforcement learning

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: directly in the real world where you have the potential to gather these large, highly

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: varied and complex data sets, you start running into other problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Like one problem you run into very quickly, it'll first sound like a very pragmatic problem,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: but it actually turns out to be a pretty deep scientific problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Take the robot, put it in your kitchen, have it try to learn to do the dishes with trial

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and error, it'll break all your dishes and then we'll have no more dishes to clean.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Now you might think this is a very practical issue, but there's something to this, which

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: is that if you have a person trying to do this, a person will have some degree of common

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: sense, they'll break one dish, they'll be a little more careful with the next one, and

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: if they break all of them, they're going to go and get more or something like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So there's all sorts of scaffolding that comes very naturally to us for our learning process.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If I have to learn something through trial and error, I have the common sense to know

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that I have to try multiple times, if I screw something up, I ask for help or I reset things

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: or something like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And all of that is kind of outside of the classic reinforcement learning problem formulation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: There are other things that can also be categorized as kind of scaffolding but are very important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: For example, where do you get your reward function?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If I want to learn how to pour a cup of water, well, how do I know if I've done it correctly?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Now that probably requires an entire computer vision system to be built just to determine

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that, and that seems a little bit inelegant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So there are all sorts of things like this that start to come up when we think through

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: what we really need to get reinforcement learning to happen at scale in the real world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And I think that many of these things actually suggest a little bit of a shortcoming in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: problem formulation and a few deeper questions that we have to resolve.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's really interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I talked to David Silver about AlphaZero, and it seems like there's no, again, we haven't

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: hit the limit at all in the context when there's no broken dishes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So in the case of Go, it's really about just scaling compute.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So again, the bottleneck is the amount of money you're willing to invest in compute

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and then maybe the different scaffolding around how difficult it is to scale compute maybe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But there, there's no limit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And it's interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Now we move to the real world and there's the broken dishes, there's all the reward

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: function like you mentioned.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's really nice.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So how do we push forward there?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Do you think there's this kind of sample efficiency question that people bring up of not having

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: to break 100,000 dishes?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Is this an algorithm question?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Is this a data selection question?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What do you think?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: How do we not break too many dishes?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Well, one way we can think about that is that maybe we need to be better at reusing our

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: data, building that iceberg.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So perhaps it's too much to hope that you can have a machine that in isolation, in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: vacuum without anything else, can just master complex tasks in minutes the way that people

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But perhaps it also doesn't have to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Perhaps what it really needs to do is have an existence, a lifetime where it does many

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: things and the previous things that it has done, prepare it to do new things more efficiently.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And the study of these kinds of questions typically falls under categories like multitask

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning or meta-learning, but they all fundamentally deal with the same general theme, which is

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: use experience for doing other things to learn to do new things efficiently and quickly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So what do you think about if you just look at the one particular case study of Tesla

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Autopilot that has quickly approaching towards a million vehicles on the road where some

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: percentage of the time, 30, 40% of the time is driving using the computer vision, multitask,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: HydroNet, right, and then the other percent, that's what they call it, HydroNet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: The other percent is human controlled.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: From the human side, how can we use that data?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's your sense?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's the signal?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Do you have ideas in this autonomous ecosystem when people can lose their lives?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's a safety critical environment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So how do we use that data?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So I think that actually the kind of problems that come up when we want systems that are

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: reliable and that can kind of understand the limits of their capabilities, they're actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: very similar to the kind of problems that come up when we're doing off-policy reinforcement

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So as I mentioned before, in off-policy reinforcement learning, the big problem is you need to know

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: when you can trust the predictions of your model because if you're trying to evaluate

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: some pattern of behavior for which your model doesn't give you an accurate prediction, then

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: you shouldn't use that to modify your policy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And it's actually very similar to the problem that we're faced when we actually then deploy

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that thing and we want to decide whether we trust it in the moment or not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So perhaps we just need to do a better job of figuring out that part, and that's a very

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: deep research question, of course, but it's also a question that a lot of people are working

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So I'm pretty optimistic that we can make some progress on that over the next few years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's the role of simulation in reinforcement learning, deep reinforcement learning, reinforcement

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Like how essential is it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's been essential for the breakthroughs so far, for some interesting breakthroughs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Do you think it's a crutch that we rely on?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I mean, again, it connects to our off-policy discussion, but do you think we can ever get

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: rid of simulation or do you think simulation will actually take over?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: We'll create more and more realistic simulations that will allow us to solve actual real-world

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: problems, like transfer the models we learn in simulation to real-world problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that simulation is a very pragmatic tool that we can use to get a lot of useful

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: stuff to work right now, but I think that in the long run, we will need to build machines

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that can learn from real data because that's the only way that we'll get them to improve

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: perpetually because if we can't have our machines learn from real data, if they have to rely

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: on simulated data, eventually the simulator becomes the bottleneck.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: In fact, this is a general thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If your machine has any bottleneck that is built by humans and that doesn't improve from

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: real data, it will eventually be the thing that holds it back.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If you're entirely reliant on your simulator, that will be the bottleneck.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If you're entirely reliant on a manually designed controller, that's going to be the bottleneck.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Simulation is very useful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's very pragmatic, but it's not a substitute for being able to utilize real experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: By the way, this is something that I think is quite relevant now, especially in the context

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of some of the things we've discussed because some of these scaffolding issues that I mentioned,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: things like the broken dishes and the unknown reward function, these are not problems that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: you would ever stumble on when working in a purely simulated environment, but they become

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: very apparent when we try to actually run these things in the real world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: To throw a brief wrench into our discussion, let me ask, do you think we're living in a

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: simulation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Oh, I have no idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Do you think that's a useful thing to even think about, about the fundamental physics

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: nature of reality?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Or another perspective, the reason I think the simulation hypothesis is interesting is

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: to think about how difficult is it to create a virtual reality game type situation that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: will be sufficiently convincing to us humans or sufficiently enjoyable that we wouldn't

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: want to leave?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I mean, that's actually a practical engineering challenge.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I personally really enjoy virtual reality, but it's quite far away, but I kind of think

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: about what would it take for me to want to spend more time in virtual reality versus

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the real world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And that's a sort of a nice clean question because at that point, if I want to live in

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: a virtual reality, that means we're just a few years away where the majority of the population

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: lives in a virtual reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And that's how we create the simulation, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You don't need to actually simulate the quantum gravity and just every aspect of the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And that's an interesting question for reinforcement learning too, is if we want to make sufficiently

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: realistic simulations that may, it blend the difference between sort of the real world

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and the simulation, thereby just some of the things we've been talking about, kind of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: problems go away if we can create actually interesting, rich simulations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's an interesting question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And it actually, I think your question casts your previous question in a very interesting

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: light, because in some ways asking whether we can, well, the more kind of practical version

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: is like, can we build simulators that are good enough to train essentially AI systems

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that will work in the world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And it's kind of interesting to think about this, about what this implies, if true, it

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: kind of implies that it's easier to create the universe than it is to create a brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And that seems like, put this way, it seems kind of weird.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: The aspect of the simulation most interesting to me is the simulation of other humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That seems to be a complexity that makes the robotics problem harder.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Now, I don't know if every robotics person agrees with that notion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Just as a quick aside, what are your thoughts about when the human enters the picture of

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the robotics problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: How does that change the reinforcement learning problem, the learning problem in general?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah, I think that's a kind of a complex question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And I guess my hope for a while had been that if we build these robotic learning systems

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that are multitask, that utilize lots of prior data, and that learn from their own experience,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the bit where they have to interact with people will be perhaps handled in much the same way

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: as all the other bits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So if they have prior experience in interacting with people, and they can learn from their

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: own experience of interacting with people for this new task, maybe that'll be enough.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Now, of course, if it's not enough, there are many other things we can do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And there's quite a bit of research in that area.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But I think it's worth a shot to see whether the multi-agent interaction, the ability to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: understand that other beings in the world have their own goals and intentions and thoughts

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and so on, whether that kind of understanding can emerge automatically from simply learning

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: to do things with and maximize utility.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That information arises from the data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You said something about gravity, that you don't need to explicitly inject anything into

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: They can be learned from the data.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And gravity is an example of something that can be learned from data, like the physics

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What are the limits of what we can learn from data?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Do you really think we can...

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So a very simple, clean way to ask that is, do you really think we can learn gravity from

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: just data, the idea, the laws of gravity?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So something that I think is a common kind of pitfall when thinking about prior knowledge

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and learning is to assume that just because we know something, then that it's better to

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: tell the machine about that rather than have it figure it out on its own.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: In many cases, things that are important that affect many of the events that the machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: will experience are actually pretty easy to learn.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If every time you drop something, it falls down, yeah, you might get the Newton's version,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: not Einstein's version, but it'll be pretty good and it will probably be sufficient for

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: you to act rationally in the world because you see the phenomena all the time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So things that are readily apparent from the data, we might not need to specify those by

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: hand.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It might actually be easier to let the machine figure them out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It just feels like there might be a space of many local minima in terms of theories

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of this world that we would discover and get stuck on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah, of course.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Newtonian mechanics is not necessarily easy to come by.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah, and in fact, in some fields of science, for example, human civilizations itself, full

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of these local optimists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So for example, if you think about how people tried to figure out biology and medicine for

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the longest time, the kind of rules, the kind of principles that serve us very well in our

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: day-to-day lives actually serve us very poorly in understanding medicine and biology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: We had kind of very superstitious and weird ideas about how the body worked until the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: advent of the modern scientific method.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So that does seem to be a failing of this approach, but it's also a failing of human

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: intelligence, arguably.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Maybe a small aside, but the idea of self-play is fascinating in reinforcement learning,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: sort of these competitive, creating a competitive context in which agents can play against each

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: other at the same skill level and thereby increasing each other's skill level.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It seems to be this kind of self-improving mechanism is exceptionally powerful in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: context where it could be applied.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: First of all, is that beautiful to you that this mechanism work as well as it does and

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: also can be generalized to other contexts like in the robotic space or anything that's

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: applicable to the real world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think that it's a very interesting idea, but I suspect that the bottleneck to actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: generalizing it to the robotic setting is actually going to be the same as the bottleneck

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: for everything else.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: We need to be able to build machines that can get better and better through natural

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: interaction with the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Once we can do that, then they can go out and play with each other, they can play with

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: people, they can play with the natural environment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But before we get there, we've got all these other problems we have to get out of the way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: There's no shortcut around that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You have to interact with the natural environment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Well, because in a self-play setting, you still need a mediating mechanism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So the reason that self-play works for a board game is because the rules of that board game

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: mediate the interaction between the agents.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So the kind of intelligent behavior that will emerge depends very heavily on the nature

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of that mediating mechanism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So on the side of reward functions, coming up with good reward functions seems to be

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the thing that we associate with general intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Human beings seem to value the idea of developing our own reward functions, of arriving at meaning

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And yet for reinforcement learning, we often specify that's the given.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: What's your sense of how we develop good reward functions?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah, I think that's a very complicated and very deep question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And you're completely right that classically in reinforcement learning, this question has

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: kind of been treated as a non-issue, that you sort of treat the reward as this external

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: thing that comes from some other bit of your biology and you kind of don't worry about

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And I do think that that's actually a little bit of a mistake that we should worry about

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And we can approach it in a few different ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: We can approach it, for instance, by thinking of reward as a communication medium.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: We can say, well, how does a person communicate to a robot what its objective is?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: We can approach it also as sort of more of an intrinsic motivation medium.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You could say, can we write down kind of a general objective that leads to good capability?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Like, for example, can you write down some objectives such that even in the absence of

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: any other task, if you maximize that objective, you'll sort of learn useful things?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: This is something that has sometimes been called unsupervised reinforcement learning,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: which I think is a really fascinating area of research, especially today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: We've done a bit of work on that recently.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: One of the things we've studied is whether we can have some notion of unsupervised reinforcement

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: learning by means of information theoretic quantities, like, for instance, minimizing

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: a Bayesian measure of surprise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: This is an idea that was pioneered actually in the computational neuroscience community

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: by folks like Carl Friston.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And we've done some work recently that shows that you can actually learn pretty interesting

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: skills by essentially behaving in a way that allows you to make accurate predictions about

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So it's all circular.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Do the things that will lead to you getting the right answer for prediction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: But by doing this, you can sort of discover stable niches in the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You can discover that if you're playing Tetris, then correctly clearing the rows will let

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: you play Tetris for longer and keep the board nice and clean, which sort of satisfies some

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: desire for order in the world, and as a result, get some degree of leverage over your domain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So we're exploring that pretty actively.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Is there a role for a human notion of curiosity in itself being the reward, sort of discovering

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: new things about the world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So one of the things that I'm pretty interested in is actually whether discovering new things

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: can actually be an emergent property of some other objective that quantifies capability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So new things for the sake of new things, maybe might not by itself be the right answer,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: but perhaps we can figure out an objective for which discovering new things is actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the natural consequence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's something we're working on right now, but I don't have a clear answer for you there

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: yet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: That's still a work in progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You mean just as a curious observation to see sort of creative patterns of curiosity

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: on the way to optimize for a particular...

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: On the way to optimize for a particular measure of capability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Is there ways to understand or anticipate unexpected, unintended consequences of particular

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: reward functions, sort of anticipate the kind of strategies that might be developed and

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: try to avoid highly detrimental strategies?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So classically, this is something that has been pretty hard in reinforcement learning

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: because it's difficult for a designer to have good intuition about what a learning

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: algorithm will come up with when they give it some objective.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: There are ways to mitigate that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: One way to mitigate it is to actually define an objective that says, don't do weird stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You can actually quantify it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: You can say just don't enter situations that have low probability under the distribution

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of states you've seen before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It turns out that that's actually one very good way to do off-policy reinforcement learning

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: actually.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So we can do some things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: If we slowly venture in speaking about reward functions into greater and greater levels

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: of intelligence, there's...

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I mean, Stuart Russell thinks about this, the alignment of AI systems with us humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: So how do we ensure that AGI systems align with us humans?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: It's kind of a reward function question of specifying the behavior of AI systems such

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: that their success aligns with the broader intended success interests of human beings.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Do you have thoughts on this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Do you have kind of concerns of where reinforcement learning fits into this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: Or are you really focused on the current moment of us being quite far away and trying to solve

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: the robotics problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I don't have a great answer to this, but...

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: And I do think that this is a problem that's important to figure out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: For my part, I'm actually a bit more concerned about the other side of this equation that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: maybe rather than unintended consequences for objectives that are specified too well,

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I'm actually more worried right now about unintended consequences for objectives that

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: are not optimized well enough, which might become a very pressing problem when we, for

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: instance, try to use these techniques for safety critical systems like cars and aircraft

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: I think at some point we'll face the issue of objectives being optimized too well, but

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: right now I think we're more likely to face the issue of them not being optimized well

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108

body.input: enough.

metadata.title: Podcast: Sergey Levine: Robotics and Machine Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #108
